Defence analysts have pointed to the devastating role cheap and plentiful drones have played in conflicts in both Ukraine and the Middle East as highlighting the vulnerability of bases like RAAF Darwin and Tindal, along with other sensitive sites like HMAS Stirling in WA — which will be the home of Australia's future nuclear-powered submarines.

Air Marshall Chappell said while there are clearly lessons from conflicts like Ukraine, Australia's geography — particularly its vast landmass, and place in the world — is worth bearing in mind.

Jets in a hanger at RAAF Base Darwin. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"The ranges and distances in the Ukraine conflict are different to the Middle East and they're different again to here in the Indo-Pacific," he said.

"So we've got to understand that what works really, really well in one theatre may have an application in another, but may not be as predominant as it is in the first theatre."

The Australian Defence Force (ADF) recently test-fired a possible new medium-range ground-based air defence system, and has said it intends to make decisions this year.

Dr Langford says that given the growing US presence at bases like RAAF Tindal, America may be willing to contribute to investment in systems like Patriot surface-to-air missile defence systems.

They have been test-fired in Australia before, but have never been adopted by the ADF.

"Some of the joint security interests between us and the US, I think, provide an opportunity for American investment," he said.

"The Patriot is very expensive. It's very effective and battle proven, but it won't answer every variable when it comes to the threat that we now face.

A Patriot air defence system in Warsaw, Poland in 2023. (Reuters: Kacper Pempel)

"As we see, particularly in the Middle East, using a $1.3 million missile to shoot down a $100,000 drone is not necessarily the most effective or affordable way to manage this counter-drone threat.

Mr Marles says that to understand US interest in Australia's north, it helps to shift perspective.

He pointed to a map published in the 2023 Defence Strategic Review that shifts the axis on which Australia is viewed, to put its proximity to South-east Asia, and north to China, in a different view.

"What you then see ahead of us is a huge proportion of the world's population, in India, China and South-east Asia, large countries," he said.

"That gives you a sense of how we are connected to the world and the significance of this theatre to the way the globe operates.

" That explains Australia's geographic significance, and it therefore explains why America has an interest here. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Man sentenced for murder of caring neighbour in Melbourne's outer-east
World.content:
A man has been sentenced after admitting to murdering his neighbour in a drug-induced stabbing frenzy when his son ran over to her house to seek refuge.

Family members of the woman stabbed to death by her neighbour, days after she baked him cupcakes, have wept as her killer was jailed.

Milorad Zaric, 48, fatally attacked Vicki Apostolopoulos and assaulted her son after chasing his own fearful son into his neighbour's property in Melbourne's outer-east.

Ms Apostolopoulos's family sat in a packed courtroom, wiping away tears throughout Zaric's sentencing in the Victorian Supreme Court today.

Justice Jacinta Forbes said the November 2024 attack was serious, and his actions took a life and irrevocably changed many others, as evidenced in the 24 victim impact statements from family, friends, neighbours and colleagues.

"This reflected the breadth of love Ms Apostolopoulos brought and the loss occasioned by her death," she said.

But Justice Forbes took into consideration Zaric's reduced moral culpability due to his ketamine-induced psychosis, deep remorse, previous good character and early guilty pleas as reasons for her to set a sentence below the standard 25 years.

She set a head sentence of 21 years and five months and a non-parole period of 14 years and six months.

Zaric, 48, had been chasing his teenage son on the morning of November 16 after abusing ketamine, cannabis and alcohol the day before.

An earlier court sketch of Milorad Zaric, who told police he had taken ketamine before the fatal attack. (ABC News: Anita Lester)

After the father punched his son, pushed the boy down the stairs and stomped on his head, the then-15-year-old boy sought refuge in Ms Apostolopoulos's home next door.

The confused neighbour let the boy inside and shut the door again.

When Zaric would not stop banging on it, she opened it and heard her killer chillingly utter: "Welcome home, Vicki."

Zaric then retrieved a knife from his waistband and plunged it into her neck, stomach and shoulder in a frenzied attack.

The Bayswater woman's own son, aged 16, grabbed Zaric in a chokehold and ordered his 12-year-old brother out of the house.

Zaric repeatedly punched the teen and slammed him against a wall, but the boy only let go to run to safety.

"You attacked a woman who had no reason to fear you," the judge said.

In the Victorian Supreme Court, Justice Jacinta Forbes said Milorad Zaric's actions took a life and irrevocably changed many others. (ABC News: Shane Willner-Browne)

The victim opened her door to Zaric in a sign of friendship, she said.

"You stabbed her with no reason, without explanation or warning."

When police arrived, he told them he had taken ketamine before growling and calling out for Satan.

Two days before the murder, Zaric had texted to thank her and praised her "amazing" cupcakes, which she had baked and taken to his house.

Defence barrister Ruth Shann SC had argued the killer's crime was out of character and his mind was altered by ketamine.

'My daughter was my life'

Ms Apostolopoulos's family had earlier called for a life sentence for her drug-addled killer.

Yesterday, Ms Apostolopoulos's sister, Mary Kadis, said Zaric's drug-addled state was no excuse for his actions.

"The choices leading up to that day were yours," she said.

"Did Vicki have a choice that day? No, she didn't."

Ms Apostolopoulos's mother, Sofia Apostolopoulos, said the grief she carried was beyond words.

"My daughter was my life," she said in a statement to the court.

"Since her death, I have been trapped in a living nightmare I cannot wake up from."

Close friend Maria Pantelios described Ms Apostolopoulos as like family.

"Her presence had a way of lifting others, even in the darkest moments," she told the court.

AAP

World.title: Tassie growers spitting chips over Simplot spud contract
World.content:
A bitter stalemate between frozen chip manufacturer Simplot and its Tasmanian suppliers has once again escalated, just weeks out from planting early potatoes for French fries.

Earlier this month, the US multinational pulled the pin on price talks for the upcoming season.

Growers rejected Simplot's proposed price reduction, resulting in a 57 per cent drop in returns for their potatoes from two years ago.

Tasmanian potato growers rejected Simplot's latest pay offer. (ABC News: Rose Grant)

Potatoes are the most valuable agriculture sector in the state, but they're also the most expensive crop to grow, costing around $25,000 a hectare or 42 cents a kilo.

The price Simplot wants to pay farmers this season is between 46 and 49 cents a kilo.

Growers threatened by Simplot's tough talk

Farmers aren't just concerned with the price, but with their treatment by Simplot.

Tractor convoy unable to break Tasmanian potato pay stalemate Tasmanian potato farmers have rejected a second pay offer from multinational processor Simplot that would see farmers paid less per kilo than last year.

The company has cut potato volumes and cancelled a number of contracts.

Then, in an unprecedented move, Simplot bypassed the grower committee that negotiates the contract on behalf of around 150 farmers.

Instead, it approached individual growers to sign incomplete contracts before they viewed a new supply agreement outlining changes to terms and conditions.

Nathan Richardson participated in a tractor convoy protest last year. (ABC News: Laurissa Smith)

Those growers were given seven days to sign the agreement, after which Simplot said it "may accept or reject at its sole discretion".

TasFarmers vegetable council chair Nathan Richardson said Simplot's behaviour is out of line.

"That's created massive pressure on the individual grower," the north-west potato farmer said.

" Operating under duress or being signed under duress is never a nice position to be put in. "

TasFarmers has raised serious concerns that Simplot bypassed the grower negotiating committee. (ABC News: Laurissa Smith)

Mr Richardson said Simplot's grower committee has also questioned the legality of the new offer.

A new condition in the agreement could also make farmers liable if there was a recall on potato chip products, even months after potatoes have left their farm.

"How we see it is that the farmer will be liable for the cost of that recall and any subsequent legal proceedings," Mr Richardson said.

"We've got to take the worst possible scenario in today's litigious world of corporatism.

Simplot supplies potato chips to Coles, Woolworth, McDonalds and KFC. (ABC Rural: Hugh Hogan)

Union linked to chip factory backing growers

Mike Wickham has been dealing with Simplot for the last 12 years as the Tasmanian organiser of the Australian Manufacturing and Workers' Union.

He said the company has indicated it'll cut back the potato volume through its Ulverstone plant by around 30,000 tonnes from its 2027 harvest.

Mike Wickham is concerned for the welfare of Ulverstone farmers and the broader community. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

"Without potatoes, there's no manufacturing of chips," Mr Wickham said.

"So, if they drive these farmers too far into the dirt with a price where its unsustainable to grow the crop, then it's a big impact on this Ulverstone site and its employees ... that's our concern."

The grower committee have approached Simplot's customers, Coles, Woolworths, McDonald's and KFC, to outline their predicament and concerns about the rise in imported potato chips.

So far, only Coles and McDonald's have responded.

Farmers have rejected a price offer made by food manufacturer Simplot for their potato crop this season. (ABC News: Laurissa Smith)

Growers say they're reluctant to speak out about Simplot's behaviour for fear of retribution.

"What a terrible feeling our growers have that, in fear of speaking out, their volume of spuds they grow, or the whole contract may be put in question by the company, " Mr Richardson said.

"I mean that is just an awful way to do business in Australia.

" It's not the Australian way. "

Yesterday, growers voted to get Simplot back to the negotiating table within the next four days. (ABC News: Meg Fergusson)

Simplot has not responded to questions for this story, but last week the company said in a statement "it rejected any suggestion it has acted inappropriately or sought to pressure growers during these discussions".

The company also said its "engagement is conducted professionally, respectfully and in good faith".

It also added that "its priority remains reaching arrangements that provide certainty for growers, support Tasmanian potato production, and help ensure the ongoing competitiveness and viability of Australia's potato processing industry".

The company has agreed to meet with the grower negotiating committee at the end of the week.

World.title: Man faces court accused of defrauding over $200,000 intended for Indigenous community
World.content:
Traditional owners giving evidence in the trial of a man accused of dishonestly appropriating and spending more than $200,000 intended for a Far North Queensland Indigenous community say they never saw any of the money.

Ankamuthi traditional owner Larry Joe Woosup has pleaded not guilty to two counts of fraud to a value of $30,000 or more each.

Crown prosecutors allege he dishonestly obtained the money intended for the Ankamuthi community.

The traditional land of the Ankamuthi people lies on north-western Cape York in Far North Queensland.

Alleged fraud

Crown prosecutor Christian Peters told Cairns District Court that about 16 years ago, Ankamuthi traditional owners, including Mr Woosup, were engaged in negotiations with mining company Gulf Alumina Limited over the ability to mine for bauxite on Ankamuthi land.

However, the negotiations had reached a stalemate by December 2009 over the company's royalties offer of 50c/tonne.

Larry Joe Woosup's trial is listed for six days in the Cairns District Court. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Mr Peters told the jury that the following year, Mr Woosup engaged a solicitor and had a trust deed written up, appointing himself as the trustee for the Ankamuthi people.

Mr Peters told the court that in 2013, Mr Woosup and another traditional owner, Beverly Tamwoy, recommenced negotiations with Gulf Alumina and later reached an agreement that included keeping the original royalties offer of 50c/tonne.

The parties signed agreements with Gulf Alumina to pay the Ankamuthi people $350,000 to be made in three payments.

The jury was told that in 2014, Mr Woosup set up an account with the Commonwealth Bank, named for the Ankamuthi people but with Mr Woosup as the only trustee and signatory.

Mr Peters said that between January 29 and February 10, 2014, Mr Woosup then drew upon the account's overdraft, withdrawing a total of $110,000, with $60,000 transferred into his personal account and $50,000 withdrawn as cash.

He said Mr Woosup did not keep any account records for what the money was spent on, even though it was required by the trust.

The prosecution also told the court that on February 24, 2014, Gulf Alumina sent Mr Woosup a cheque for $95,000 as part of the agreement, which he deposited into another trust account he had opened with Queensland Country Credit Union.

Mr Woosup was also the sole trustee of that account, the court heard.

Mr Peters said Mr Woosup withdrew nearly the entire contents of the account between February 27 and April 30 of that year, again without keeping records of what the money was spent on.

Crown witnesses

Crown witnesses and Ankamuthi traditional owners gave evidence today, with each saying they did not receive money from Mr Woosup in 2014 as part of the Gulf Alumina deal.

Tracy Lee Lutwych told the court that she asked Mr Woosup in 2015 about rumours he had taken money as part of a mining deal.

She said he replied: "I would not do that to my family."

Parts of Cape York have become known for their large bauxite deposits. (ABC: Richard Dinnen)

Polly Josephine Woosup said that in a conversation she witnessed in 2018, her uncle Mark Gebadi told Mr Woosup that the money Mr Woosup took belonged to the Ankamuthi people.

Mr Peters asked: "Did Larry respond, 'We should leave that behind us, that's only a small amount and we've got more money coming toward us?'"

Ms Woosup responded: "Yes."

Another witness, Amanda Ewart, told the court she received a chain text message from Mr Woosup in 2018, in which he said he had taken $30,000 and given $10,000 to Beverly Tamwoy.

Under cross-examination from Mr Woosup's counsel, barrister Matt Jackson asked Ms Ewart if she agreed that, outside of the text messages, Mr Woosup never said he had used the money from Gulf Alumina on himself.

Ms Ewart said that was not true.

"We had board meetings where he was explaining the situation and his entitlement to that money as Ankamuthi head of the family," she said.

Kevin Wone, an accountant Mr Woosup used during the negotiations with Gulf Alumina, told the court during his evidence that he was not aware of Mr Woosup's trust accounts.

The jury was also shown a police document with Mr Woosup's responses to questions about a $10,000 cash withdrawal when he said he had given the money to Mr Wone for accountancy fees.

Mr Wone told the court that he never received the money.

The trial before Judge Joshua Treviño KC is set down for more than six days.

World.title: Inquiry finds Catholic school discriminated against staff over sexual orientation
World.content:
A two-year-long parliamentary inquiry into bullying and discrimination within Tasmanian schools has published its final report, with its chair declaring that "at the heart of this inquiry is pain".

But despite the inquiry's broad range, chair and Labor MP Brian Mitchell said he predicted the public focus would be on the committee's findings on the bullying and discrimination faced by LGBTIQA+ students in the state's Catholic schools.

The inquiry was initiated by independent MP Kristie Johnston in June 2024, following the release of national data that found Tasmania had the highest rates of schoolyard bullying in the country.

Among its 55 findings, the final report found Catholic Education Tasmania, which operates 39 Tasmanian schools, discriminated against staff based on sexual orientation and marital status, contravening the state anti-discrimination laws — but noted the assertion has not been determined in court.

Brian Mitchell chaired the Inquiry into Discrimination and Bullying in Tasmanian Schools. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"There will be criticism from some quarters that the inquiry has focused too intently on Catholic education and targets religious freedom, etc", Mr Mitchell said.

"Such criticism is simplistic, unfair and untrue."

The criticism Mr Mitchell anticipated emerged within the report itself, with two inquiry committee members, Tasmanian government MPs Michael Ferguson and Mark Shelton, issuing a joint dissenting statement.

While the two MPs strongly agreed that every student should be safe at school, they were concerned the report went too far in responding to discrimination and bullying with respect to gender identity and faith-based education.

"Faith-based education should not be misrepresented as though religious beliefs (Christian or otherwise) and student wellbeing are at odds with each other," they said.

MPs Mark Shelton (left) and Michael Ferguson (back right) issued a joint dissenting statement, which appeared in the report. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Labor member Anita Dow, Greens member Vica Bayley, and independents Ms Johnston and Helen Burnet also sat on the committee.

Calls for anti-discrimination laws to be reviewed

The inquiry was established with a scope to report on discrimination, bullying and harassment in Tasmanian schools; to examine the impact of discrimination and bullying on a student's educational outcome; and to determine whether legislative or policy reforms are needed.

The report, which was delayed due to a snap state election last year, detailed the "real and persistent" discrimination and harassment within the state's education system.

It found bullying, harassment and discrimination remained significant issues within schools, despite the anti-bullying policies in place across the sector.

It highlighted shortcomings in support, training, mental health care, data collection and policy. The report also noted LGBTIQA+ students and students with disabilities were disproportionately affected by bullying, harassment and discrimination.

The report made 33 recommendations, including a blanket call for "all schools" to implement anti-discrimination and anti-bullying policies, and for the state to review its anti-discrimination legislation.

The inquiry received 294 submissions, and heard from 47 witnesses over seven public hearings and several confidential hearings.

Many of the submissions were sent from parents with children attending "a Christian school", and whose submissions appeared to have been prepared by the website OneClickPolitics.

The website states it provides "innovative and easy-to-use digital solutions to amplify your advocates' voices with the goal of impacting policy outcomes".

Employment practices lawful, school body says

Mr Mitchell said the inquiry had not been a review into the merits or otherwise of faith-based education.

"It is simply a fact that evidence was presented relating to the negative experiences of young LGBTIQA+ people in faith-based, particularly Catholic, schools," he said.

Among those the inquiry heard from was Sam Johnstone, a former deputy principal of Marist Regional College in Burnie, who told the inquiry he was stood down from the Catholic secondary school after disclosing a de facto relationship.

It also heard from a Year 12 transgender girl, Amilie Courtney, who attended the Catholic co-educational St Patrick's College in Launceston.

She told the inquiry she had been the subject of segregation and bullying, describing herself as "a problem to be managed, separated and restricted".

Amilie Courtney spoke at the parliamentary inquiry about her experience as a transgender schoolgirl. (Supplied: Parliament of Tasmania)

Catholic Education Tasmania told the parliamentary inquiry that it denies senior leadership positions to staff who aren't in "regular" relationships or who are homosexual.

It said it was protected under, and compliant with, the federal Sex Discrimination Act.

The LGBTIQA+ advocacy group Equality Tasmania said at the time it was concerned this was in breach of the state's anti-discrimination laws.

The report found Tasmanian and Commonwealth anti-discrimination legislation "operate concurrently, with their application into matters of employment in faith-based schools not yet determined before a court of law".

The inquiry was initiated by Kristie Johnston in June 2024. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Ms Johnston said the finding that Catholic Education Tasmania discriminated against staff on the basis of sexual orientation and marital status was a test for the state government.

"Will it stand by its gold-class anti-discrimination legislation and take up the fight on behalf of Tasmanians experiencing discrimination, because in Tasmania we don't discriminate," Mr Johnston said.

" Will it stand up to the Catholic church? "

Equality Tasmania spokesperson Rodney Croome and Ms Johnston said they would refer the report to Tasmania's anti-discrimination commissioner.

In a statement, Catholic Education Tasmania said it would continue to review and improve its educational environments and support systems for students, family and staff.

Its executive director, Dr Terry McCarthy, said he was confident the organisation's employment practices were lawful.

World.title: Powerhouse Parramatta announces chef for waterfront restaurant, cafe and wine bar
World.content:
Eating outRestaurant news Powerhouse Parramatta announces chef for waterfront restaurant, cafe and wine bar His Gladesville restaurant is a favourite haunt of RecipeTin Eats’ Nagi Maehashi and he’ll be drawing on his years of working at Aria, Chiswick and Opera Bar. Boronia Kitchen chef-restaurateur Simon Sandall has been appointed retail food and beverage operator at Powerhouse Parramatta. Boronia Kitchen chef-restaurateur Simon Sandall will lead the hospitality offering at Powerhouse Parramatta, which opens its landmark $950 million facility with a waterfront restaurant, cinema bar and cafe-wine bar on Saturday, November 7. The UK-born chef said the appointment was the highlight of his 41-year career in hospitality: “I sometimes questioned – not in a bad way – why I was here in Australia, and when I got this I realised why. It’s a massive personal milestone.” Sandall is no stranger to big-name venues. Before opening his Gladesville restaurant Boronia Kitchen in 2018, he worked for celebrity chef Matt Moran – first as the head chef at hatted Circular Quay restaurant Aria; then as group executive chef, overseeing popular venues such as Chiswick and Opera Bar. At Boronia Kitchen, Sandall’s contemporary Australian menu and considered-but-casual service caught the attention of Australia’s most popular food-blogger, Nagi Maehashi of RecipeTin Eats and Good Food contributor, who described the restaurant as “exactly the sort of place I’d want if I ever, one day, have my own restaurant”.



“It’s incredible, she’s a massive advocate of Boronia Kitchen,” Sandall said. “What I love about Nagi is that you know if she likes something and you know if she doesn’t.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Powerhouse Parramatta is set to open in November. Rory Gardiner The restaurant at Powerhouse Parramatta is more than double the capacity of Boronia Kitchen, with an indoor-outdoor dining area capable of seating about 290 people. It features a minimal industrial aesthetic, similar to the rest of the museum, with concrete floors, aluminium accents and a series of stools and tables fabricated from cork and stainless steel, designed by Adam Goodrum in Sydney. Sandall said he was approached with the opportunity to become the Powerhouse Parramatta retail food and beverage operator while consulting on the museum’s catering facilities. Sandall established Aria Catering and has run his own catering business, Catering by Simon Sandall, alongside Boronia Kitchen since 2022. “A couple of people reached out and said, you know, you should have a crack at it,” he said. Sandall was intrigued – according to the NSW government, Powerhouse Parramatta is the most significant infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House, where Sandall got his first kitchen job when he landed in Sydney, back in 1995.



“I’m getting goosebumps now, talking about it,” Sandall said. “For me, it’s the excitement of what western Sydney is becoming.” Diners outside Boronia Kitchen, Gladesville. Leigh Griffiths When it opens, Powerhouse Parramatta will have an extensive food program, including farmers’ markets, demonstration kitchens and apartments for international chef residencies. The museum hired renowned chef-restaurateur Kylie Kwong as an associate for its food department in 2024, and her work with western Sydney chefs and food businesses further cemented its focus on local cuisine, showcasing underrepresented voices in hospitality. While the name of the restaurant remains under wraps for now, Sandall said its menu will be similar in style to Boronia Kitchen’s: quality produce, presented simply, with diverse culinary influence and broad appeal. A lot of cooking will be done on a wood-fired grill, and Sandall has started collaborating with Powerhouse horticulturalists as they develop the on-site working garden, requesting finger lime, warrigal green and yuzu plants. “It will be an extension of Boronia Kitchen because that’s me, you know, that’s the food I like to eat and cook, but it will probably be a little bit more culturally diverse,” he said.



“It’s going to be highly punchy, full of flavour and fresh.” Boronia Kitchen will not be affected by the appointment. Further information on the cafe and bars to come.

World.title: ‘Wake-up call for us’: Waratahs brace for change after Cheika return is confirmed
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘Wake-up call for us’: Waratahs brace for change after Cheika return is confirmed Iain Payten Updated August 19, 2026 — 5:32pm ,first published 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Waratahs say the return of Michael Cheika for as little as one season is not a “sugar hit” and the former Wallabies coach will set up the battling franchise for long-term success with his strong coaching beliefs and structures. Confirming this masthead’s report on Monday, Cheika was officially announced as the Waratahs’ new head coach on Wednesday, after signing on for a return to the franchise he led to a Super Rugby title in 2014. It remains the Waratahs’ one and only premiership. Michael Cheika has been on the Roosters’ full-time staff in 2026. Getty Cheika is joining the franchise on a two-year deal, in which the 59-year-old will lead the Tahs in 2027 but potentially then exit in 2028, and instead pass the baton to a senior assistant coach, who is yet to be appointed. Former Wallaby and Waratah Stephen Hoiles is in discussions with the Waratahs and owners Rugby Australia. Cheika coached the Waratahs between 2013 and 2015, winning the competition in the second season and making the semi-finals in the third. The Waratahs and RA hope Cheika can turn the club around and reignite passion for the team among the growing number of fans who have lost interest in Super Rugby and the Tahs.



The recruitment comes after coach Dan McKellar exited the troubled franchise in June. Cheika will begin at the Waratahs in November after finishing with the Roosters, where he is currently an assistant coach, and then leading Lebanon to the Rugby League World Cup. Out of respect for the Roosters, Cheika did not front media on Wednesday but said in a statement the opportunity to return to the Tahs had a special pull. Michael Cheika talks to Roosters outside back Cody Ramsey. Getty Images “The NSW Waratahs have always occupied a special place for me – it’s my home state and I feel ready to return as their head coach ahead of an important year for the Waratahs and also for Australian rugby in the lead up to the home Rugby World Cup,” Cheika said in a statement. “Being involved in the NSW squad that lifted the Super Rugby trophy in 2014 is something I will never forget, especially the passion and energy of our supporters. This is a new time, a different time, and I am looking forward to being able to enjoy those same kinds of feelings and more with players, their families and all the fans in this new adventure.”



Waratahs head of high performance Barrie-Jon Mather said he hoped Cheika’s record as a turnaround specialist would yield good results at the Waratahs. “He usually gets a good bounce when he comes into a club,” Mather said. “So we have a really talented squad and a young squad. We brought some experience in around that. So I think ‘Cheik’ probably backs himself to get that performance bounce in the very near future.” Michael Cheika and Michael Hooper celebrate victory over the Crusaders in the Super Rugby decider in 2014. Getty Images With a big profile as a former title winner and fiery ex-Wallabies coach, Cheika will undoubtedly reignite the interest of Waratahs fans, and the broader sporting landscape, too. Mather denied Cheika would be a short-term “sugar hit” for the franchise, however.



“If you know him ... he’s not here for a sugar hit. He’ll have a lot to say and a lot of things, and he’ll steer that direction pretty well,” Mather said. “He’s got some fairly firm beliefs, in how the game is played and what success looks like, and that’s what we really want from him. “It [the Waratahs environment] will have some direction, that’s for sure. He’s very clear on how he wants things done, and it might be a bit of a wake-up call for some of us in terms of how we do things. That track record of success buys you that ability to do that.” Cheika’s coaching staff is yet to be finalised, but former 2014 Waratah back-rower Wycliff Palu is a chance to also return as an assistant. Tom Carter, Locky McCaffrey and Dan Palmer are on the existing staff and on contract for next year, but Mather said the reality is that some change is likely. Cheika’s exit from the Wallabies in 2019 was acrimonious, and he conceded later he had poor relationships with then chief executive Raelene Castle and chairman Cameron Clyne. Waugh was on the RA board at the time, but Mather said none of that history was a problem during negotiations seven years later.



“They say time heals all wounds – it’s a long time ago when he left and there’s a lot of water under the bridge. So when his name came up in conversations, there were never any sort of major obstacles raised as a red flag not to have that conversation and see if he was interested and vice versa from Cheik,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Super Rugby Back in blue: Cheika set to return as Waratahs coach A believer in there can only be one boss, Cheika said in 2020 he “should have quit” when Scott Johnson was appointed above him as director of rugby above him in 2019. Asked if he believed Cheika could work within an organisational structure of RA sitting above the Waratahs as owners, Mather said: “All head coaches want full control, don’t they? But like most things, there’s always limits to what that full control actually looks like. We’re working within a structure with RA and Michael knows exactly what he’s coming into.” Cheika is not the only 2014 Waratah returning, with Bernard Foley and Nick Phipps having also signed for a season in 2027. Roosters back-rower Angus Crichton is also coming across to the Waratahs.



Suaalii positional shift flagged in Wallabies squad for Argentina Coach Les Kiss has flagged a potential move for Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii into the Wallabies’ back three after the NSW superstar was cleared to return from a hamstring injury for the two-Test tour of Argentina. Kiss released a largely unchanged Wallabies squad on Wednesday for the series with the Pumas, which will see them clash in San Salvador de Jujuy on August 30 and Mendoza on September 6. Loading The two major additions from the Wallabies squads that downed Japan in Osaka and Townsville were Len Ikitau, who missed both games with an ankle injury, and Suaalii, who was out from the big win at the weekend in Townsville with a hamstring problem.



In an interesting twist, however, one of the men who dropped out the squad to make room for the star duo was fullback Jock Campbell, just a few days after the 31-year-old was named as Queensland’s best player. Campbell started for the Wallabies in the first Test of the year against Ireland before being contentiously moved to the bench for the Test against France in Brisbane, where he was used as a five-eighth. Campbell has since not featured for the Wallabies. After coming in for Suaalii in Townsville, Josh Flook also dropped out of the squad, but Kiss has not made room for Ikitau and Suaalii by dropping any other of his centres; namely Hunter Paisami and Isaac Henry. Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii celebrate after Max Jorgensen’s winning try in 2024. AP Both turned in outstanding performances for the Wallabies as a starting midfield in Townsville, with Henry playing strongly at No.13 in his run-on debut.



His form prompted questions post-game about whether Suaalii might be looked at as a winger or fullback. The omission of Campbell suggests Kiss may be considering that for the Argentina trip. Kiss moved Suaalii to wing in Osaka when Henry entered the game in the second half. Tom Wright is the starting fullback, but with Campbell gone, the back-up would be between Max Jorgensen, Suaalii and Ben Donaldson. In other news, Tom Hooper has also been named in the squad, and as forecast, Taniela Tupou will also tour Argentina. The pair play for overseas clubs but are remaining with the Wallabies under World Rugby’s regulation 9. The rule allows the mandatory release of players by clubs for Test rugby.



With one more game of a suspension to serve, Miles Amatosero was also left out. Kiss said in statement: “As coaches we’ve looked to maintain consistency in selection with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks, through their hard work and connection on and off the field. “Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it’s one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Construction boss accused of plotting standover in secret sushi shop meeting with bikies
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Construction boss accused of plotting standover in secret sushi shop meeting with bikies Nick McKenzie Updated August 19, 2026 — 5:26pm ,first published 11:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A senior executive of Australian infrastructure giant BMD has been accused of secretly meeting violent members of a Melbourne bikie gang in a Brisbane sushi restaurant as part of a plot to threaten a CFMEU activist blamed for causing problems on an Albanese government-funded project. The revelations have prompted the Labor-backed CFMEU administrator, Michael Crosby, to issue a fresh call for government action to combat the “complete failure of the regulatory system” and to call on companies with alleged links to bikie gangs and the underworld to clean up their backyards. BMD manager Robert Pickard has also been accused in a Queensland inquiry of attempting to cover up the incident after the CFMEU crane driver complained that the leader of a three-man Melbourne bikie crew had threatened to burn down his house and murder his family during a subsequent confrontation on the $350 million Centenary Bridge project. Counsel assisting the Queensland Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU, Eddy Gisonda, KC, suggested on Wednesday afternoon that the terrifying standover incident occurred a short time after Pickard had met the bikie trio at a sushi shop a short stroll from the bridge redevelopment.



Related Article Building Bad ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies But while being questioned by Gisonda, Pickard repeatedly denied allegations that he knew of or witnessed the alleged Comanchero gang standover on June 5, 2024. He also dismissed suggestions he had met the bikies at the sushi shop or coordinated the alleged standover with the owner of BMD’s security subcontractor, Melbourne company Host. Pickard’s denials came after Gisonda presented a detailed circumstantial case to back up his accusation that Pickard and BMD’s human resources chief, Steve Thomas, appeared to have played a key role in the suspected Comanchero standover of CFMEU-affiliated crane driver Cody Raymond, a man blamed for helping the construction union target BMD. Evidence aired by Gisonda before Commissioner Stuart Wood included receipts showing that one of the three bikies had purchased sushi just minutes after Pickard and Thomas had placed orders at the sushi shop. A short time after that, Pickard and Thomas can be seen on CCTV walking towards the Centenary Bridge project as they are trailed by three Comancheros and Melbourne businessman Gary Samuel, the BMD security subcontractor who was hired to counter an aggressive campaign by the CFMEU targeting BMD.



Pickard disagreed with Gisonda’s suggestion that he and Thomas had led the bikies to the work site at a distance to “to make sure the coast was clear” before Raymond was approached and threatened. Phone data presented by Gisonda also revealed repeated contact or attempted contact between Samuel and both Pickard and Thomas around the time Samuel was picking up the three Melbourne bikies from Brisbane airport, as well as just after what the barrister alleged was a secret rendezvous at the sushi outlet. During the hearing, Wood appeared to accept that Samuel had engineered the bikie standover in retaliation for the conduct of the CFMEU. “It makes sense for Mr Samuel to do this,” Wood suggested, referring to the use of the three feared bikie identities.



“It might be quite unlawful ... [but he had been] taking a knife to a gun fight and he wants to improve the tactics” in respect of BMD’s strategy, he said, to resist CFMEU pressure and in light of the indifference of state authorities to union conduct. “I am not saying it excuses him … But it gives a rational explanation for what he did,” Wood said of Samuel. Rob Pickard (right), General Manager, Queensland and Northern Territory, BMD Constructions is seen being questioned by Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC (left) during the Commission of Inquiry. AAPIMAGE During the hearing, Wood also queried why BMD had told police in November 2024 that CCTV of the bikie incident was no longer available, given the company had provided the vision to Wood’s commission earlier this year. Wood also asked Gisonda to make inquiries about whether it was unlawful for a company or person to “deliberately or inadvertently mislead the police”. But Pickard dismissed the claim that he or BMD were party to a bikie threat plot or that Pickard had sought to “deflect” attention away from his own or Samuel’s role in allegedly coordinating the potentially criminal act.



Wednesday’s hearing will ultimately inform Wood as he weighs whether the circumstantial evidence gathered by Gisonda and the Queensland Police investigators assisting his inquiry is strong enough to allow Wood to make an adverse finding about Pickard or BMD’s involvement in the bikie plot. Gisonda opened the hearing on Wednesday by revealing that law enforcement agencies suspected the Comancheros of seeking to build a construction empire via front companies and by infiltrating union ranks. Queensland’s Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU has laid bare the involvement of the Comancheros in the construction industry. Getty Images He claimed police intelligence, including extensive phone data, indicated the Comanchero bikie gang had in early 2024 embarked on a concerted effort to do this in both Victoria and Queensland. According to Gisonda, this effort involved the now former Melbourne-based Comanchero boss Bemir Saracevic. Saracevic is the same bikie figure Gisonda identified as allegedly leading the standover of Raymond.



Gisonda also tabled union-backed enterprise bargaining agreements allegedly secured by Comanchero-linked building firms in Victoria, including an EBA signed off by the CFMEU administration last month and by the Australian Workers’ Union in 2025. A separate investigation by The Age has established that basic due diligence should have revealed to both unions that these firms had business links to the Comancheros: one had previously been refused a licence to operate by Victoria’s Labour Hire Authority, while both had clear links to the wife of Saracevic. Bemir Saracevic. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU In a statement, Crosby told this masthead that the EBA his union had recently granted a firm now alleged to be Comanchero-linked was intended to protect workers. The CFMEU administrator said it was up to government, and not the CFMEU, to prevent underworld infiltration. “The Administrator has called for a Fit and Proper Persons Test to be applied to participants in the construction industry. It’s time the industry was cleaned up. It’s time to stop blaming workers for the complete failure of the regulatory system. It’s not the job of the union to clean up the industry,” he said.



“We’ll clean up our backyard – it’s time for employers to clean up theirs.” Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad ‘Idiots in Victoria’ holding back CFMEU: Administrator blasts former union bosses, demands reform The Queensland hearing has also placed immense scrutiny on BMD, which is currently working on Victoria’s Eastern Freeway upgrade and other Big Build projects. In Sydney, it is working on the new international airport in Western Sydney. In July, the Crisafulli government in Queensland announced that BMD had won the contract to undertake early works for the new Brisbane Stadium Olympics venue. Asked by this masthead about the evidence heard at the commission suggesting BMD associated with underworld-linked figures in the alleged Centenary Bridge stand-over incident and whether BMD’s internal investigation into the matter was adequate, the company’s spokesperson said: “BMD has additional representatives to appear over the coming days and it would be premature for us to comment.”



When Thomas, BMD’s human resources chief, gave evidence to the commission on Wednesday afternoon, he also denied being aware of the three bikie figures as they and Samuel appeared to trail Pickard and the human resources manager as they walked towards the location where Raymond was confronted. Thomas insisted he had not witnessed or had any prior knowledge of the bikie gang activity on June 5. Thomas, who will give further evidence on Thursday, also defended his failure to provide CCTV of the incident to the QLD Police when they first sought it in late 2024. “I took all reasonable steps to locate that footage at that time… I wasn’t able to locate that footage,” Thomas said. The revelations at the Queensland inquiry give Australians a taste of what is likely to be unveiled at the promised and upcoming Victorian royal commission. Many of the key subjects discussed at this week’s hearings in Brisbane are from Melbourne and are variously entrenched in both Victoria’s underworld and its building sector. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Jockey Tim Clark will be out to make it a third Listed Pioneer Services Rowley Mile (1600m) in recent years when partnering the Anthony and Sam Freedman-trained Punch Lane in Thursday’s $200,000 feature. Clark won the event on Gaulois in 2019 and Arbeitsam in 2017, and has high hopes that Punch Lane can repeat the dose. Jockey Tim Clark. Getty Images “It profiles as a nice race for him,” said Clark, who has been aboard Punch Lane in trackwork. “He likes getting his toe in the ground so the prospect of a rain-affected track is in his favour.



“The mile suits and from the wide draw there’s a good straight run to try and get a spot.” Punch Lane was a last-start fourth in the Winter Challenge at Rosehill behind Midnight Dynamite, which Clark will ride in Saturday’s Group 1 Winx Stakes at Randwick. “It was a good run by Punch Lane in that event,” Clark said. “He held on pretty well and he’s had a trial since so he’s ready to go.” Clark will combine with the Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott-prepared Tempestuous when it resumes from a lengthy spell in the Peter Smith Memorial Super Maiden Plate (1100m).



“He was off the scene for a long time after showing ability as a two-year-old,” said Clark. “Steel Will made the form look good when winning at Rosehill last Saturday.” Clark has two other rides at Hawkesbury with both being for trainer Sara Ryan. World.title: Health minister agrees to investigation into beleaguered Concord hospital
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWDoctors at work Health minister agrees to investigation into beleaguered Concord hospital Rachel Rasker August 19, 2026 — 4:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NSW Auditor-General’s office will investigate allegations of targeted disciplinary action within Sydney Local Health District in what appears to be a last-ditch effort to fend off a mutiny among Concord Hospital staff. Health Minister Ryan Park agreed to the probe one day before senior doctors in the hospital’s Medical Staff Council (MSC) were due to hold a vote of no confidence in NSW Health leadership and demand a parliamentary inquiry into the NSW health ministry. Dr Raoul Pope was disciplined by NSW Health following social media posts. Wolter Peeters The doctors’ demands, fuelled by the suspension of outspoken spinal neurosurgeon Dr Raoul Pope, threatened to spark a statewide revolt among public hospital clinicians fed up with alleged widespread governance failures and a lack of accountability within NSW Health. In an email sent to members of the MSC on Wednesday and seen by the Herald, former chair Dr Winston Cheung said Minister Park agreed to an investigation into the disciplinary processes at Concord.



Related Article Doctors at work Sydney doctors plan revolt against NSW Health “We have been asking for an independent, external investigation into aspects of governance for four years, and finally this request has been actioned,” the email read. “The scope of the investigation will be determined by the NSW Auditor-General without interference by the government or NSW Health.” Cheung said he expected the investigation would examine any allegations of a “weaponisation” of policy to discipline staff who have raised concerns. Cheung’s email counselled that the vote of no confidence should not proceed on Thursday. In July, this masthead revealed that Pope had received a disciplinary letter from the hospital’s people and culture team about his emails and LinkedIn activity, which were critical of hospital management.



Pope was told his actions were “undermining staff confidence in leadership” and “inconsistent with your obligations to protect the reputation and interests of SLHD and NSW Health”. Following the Herald’s article, Pope was suspended without pay from his role as visiting medical officer at Concord. The disciplinary action was “a risk management measure” due to “risks to staff or patient health, safety or welfare”, the people and culture team advised in an internal memo seen by the Herald. An Instagram video of Greens health spokesperson Dr Amanda Cohn sharing the news of the Pope’s suspension in parliament amassed more than 300,000 views this month and was widely circulated among clinicians, adding pressure on the government.



“Why do essential frontline health workers continue to be punished by this government for their advocacy for better health services?” Cohn said in the clip. In a statement, Cohn said the Auditor-General’s investigation was an “important acknowledgement of the seriousness of the issues that frontline staff have been raising, and a valuable next step”. Senior doctors at Concord Hospital have raised concerns about what they call widespread workplace issues. James Brickwood Cohn said she would still pursue a wider parliamentary inquiry. “Health care workers must feel safe and supported to be able to raise issues about their workplace and patients’ safety,” she said.



Related Article Healthcare Delayed cancer diagnoses, broken bones missed: The patients caught up in a Sydney hospital fail “Suppression of their voices by NSW Health is not an isolated or local issue [to Concord], and I am optimistic that a parliamentary inquiry will be able to examine this broader problem.” In Cheung’s email to doctors, he said he hoped the staff who had “resigned or who have suffered will finally get justice and closure”. He called the meeting with Park “very constructive” and said the group – which also included the MSC chairs of Canterbury Hospital and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital – discussed issues including resourcing, staffing and the social media policy. Both the doctors’ union and opposition MPs have criticised the social media policy, introduced by NSW Health in November last year.



When questioned in a budget estimates hearing on Wednesday, Fatima Abbas, the deputy secretary of people, culture and governance at NSW Health, said the policy was not designed to suppress freedom of communication. “The intent is not to discourage appropriate discourse or discussions about issues,” she said. Abbas could not answer how many clinicians had been suspended under the policy, as she said the information was not collected centrally. In his email, Cheung said he looked forward to “the truth-telling that this investigation will allow”. “We should wait for the terms of reference for the investigation from the Auditor-General before making any further decisions on this matter, but I expect this engagement from them will only be positive,” it read. Park and the Sydney Local Health District have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Powerhouse Parramatta announces chef for waterfront restaurant, cafe and wine bar
World.content:
Eating outRestaurant news Powerhouse Parramatta announces chef for waterfront restaurant, cafe and wine bar His Gladesville restaurant is a favourite haunt of RecipeTin Eats’ Nagi Maehashi and he’ll be drawing on his years of working at Aria, Chiswick and Opera Bar. Bianca Hrovat August 19, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Boronia Kitchen chef-restaurateur Simon Sandall has been appointed retail food and beverage operator at Powerhouse Parramatta. Boronia Kitchen chef-restaurateur Simon Sandall will lead the hospitality offering at Powerhouse Parramatta, which opens its landmark $950 million facility with a waterfront restaurant, cinema bar and cafe-wine bar on Saturday, November 7. The UK-born chef said the appointment was the highlight of his 41-year career in hospitality: “I sometimes questioned – not in a bad way – why I was here in Australia, and when I got this I realised why. It’s a massive personal milestone.” Sandall is no stranger to big-name venues. Before opening his Gladesville restaurant Boronia Kitchen in 2018, he worked for celebrity chef Matt Moran – first as the head chef at hatted Circular Quay restaurant Aria; then as group executive chef, overseeing popular venues such as Chiswick and Opera Bar. At Boronia Kitchen, Sandall’s contemporary Australian menu and considered-but-casual service caught the attention of Australia’s most popular food-blogger, Nagi Maehashi of RecipeTin Eats and Good Food contributor, who described the restaurant as “exactly the sort of place I’d want if I ever, one day, have my own restaurant”.



“It’s incredible, she’s a massive advocate of Boronia Kitchen,” Sandall said. “What I love about Nagi is that you know if she likes something and you know if she doesn’t.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Powerhouse Parramatta is set to open in November. Rory Gardiner The restaurant at Powerhouse Parramatta is more than double the capacity of Boronia Kitchen, with an indoor-outdoor dining area capable of seating about 290 people. It features a minimal industrial aesthetic, similar to the rest of the museum, with concrete floors, aluminium accents and a series of stools and tables fabricated from cork and stainless steel, designed by Adam Goodrum in Sydney. Sandall said he was approached with the opportunity to become the Powerhouse Parramatta retail food and beverage operator while consulting on the museum’s catering facilities. Sandall established Aria Catering and has run his own catering business, Catering by Simon Sandall, alongside Boronia Kitchen since 2022. “A couple of people reached out and said, you know, you should have a crack at it,” he said. Sandall was intrigued – according to the NSW government, Powerhouse Parramatta is the most significant infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House, where Sandall got his first kitchen job when he landed in Sydney, back in 1995.



“I’m getting goosebumps now, talking about it,” Sandall said. “For me, it’s the excitement of what western Sydney is becoming.” Diners outside Boronia Kitchen, Gladesville. Leigh Griffiths When it opens, Powerhouse Parramatta will have an extensive food program, including farmers’ markets, demonstration kitchens and apartments for international chef residencies. The museum hired renowned chef-restaurateur Kylie Kwong as an associate for its food department in 2024, and her work with western Sydney chefs and food businesses further cemented its focus on local cuisine, showcasing underrepresented voices in hospitality. While the name of the restaurant remains under wraps for now, Sandall said its menu will be similar in style to Boronia Kitchen’s: quality produce, presented simply, with diverse culinary influence and broad appeal. A lot of cooking will be done on a wood-fired grill, and Sandall has started collaborating with Powerhouse horticulturalists as they develop the on-site working garden, requesting finger lime, warrigal green and yuzu plants. “It will be an extension of Boronia Kitchen because that’s me, you know, that’s the food I like to eat and cook, but it will probably be a little bit more culturally diverse,” he said.



“It’s going to be highly punchy, full of flavour and fresh.” Boronia Kitchen will not be affected by the appointment. Further information on the cafe and bars to come.

World.title: ‘Wake-up call for us’: Waratahs brace for change after Cheika return is confirmed
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘Wake-up call for us’: Waratahs brace for change after Cheika return is confirmed Iain Payten Updated August 19, 2026 — 5:32pm ,first published 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Waratahs say the return of Michael Cheika for as little as one season is not a “sugar hit” and the former Wallabies coach will set up the battling franchise for long-term success with his strong coaching beliefs and structures. Confirming this masthead’s report on Monday, Cheika was officially announced as the Waratahs’ new head coach on Wednesday, after signing on for a return to the franchise he led to a Super Rugby title in 2014. It remains the Waratahs’ one and only premiership. Michael Cheika has been on the Roosters’ full-time staff in 2026. Getty Cheika is joining the franchise on a two-year deal, in which the 59-year-old will lead the Tahs in 2027 but potentially then exit in 2028, and instead pass the baton to a senior assistant coach, who is yet to be appointed. Former Wallaby and Waratah Stephen Hoiles is in discussions with the Waratahs and owners Rugby Australia. Cheika coached the Waratahs between 2013 and 2015, winning the competition in the second season and making the semi-finals in the third. The Waratahs and RA hope Cheika can turn the club around and reignite passion for the team among the growing number of fans who have lost interest in Super Rugby and the Tahs.



The recruitment comes after coach Dan McKellar exited the troubled franchise in June. Cheika will begin at the Waratahs in November after finishing with the Roosters, where he is currently an assistant coach, and then leading Lebanon to the Rugby League World Cup. Out of respect for the Roosters, Cheika did not front media on Wednesday but said in a statement the opportunity to return to the Tahs had a special pull. Michael Cheika talks to Roosters outside back Cody Ramsey. Getty Images “The NSW Waratahs have always occupied a special place for me – it’s my home state and I feel ready to return as their head coach ahead of an important year for the Waratahs and also for Australian rugby in the lead up to the home Rugby World Cup,” Cheika said in a statement. “Being involved in the NSW squad that lifted the Super Rugby trophy in 2014 is something I will never forget, especially the passion and energy of our supporters. This is a new time, a different time, and I am looking forward to being able to enjoy those same kinds of feelings and more with players, their families and all the fans in this new adventure.”



Waratahs head of high performance Barrie-Jon Mather said he hoped Cheika’s record as a turnaround specialist would yield good results at the Waratahs. “He usually gets a good bounce when he comes into a club,” Mather said. “So we have a really talented squad and a young squad. We brought some experience in around that. So I think ‘Cheik’ probably backs himself to get that performance bounce in the very near future.” Michael Cheika and Michael Hooper celebrate victory over the Crusaders in the Super Rugby decider in 2014. Getty Images With a big profile as a former title winner and fiery ex-Wallabies coach, Cheika will undoubtedly reignite the interest of Waratahs fans, and the broader sporting landscape, too. Mather denied Cheika would be a short-term “sugar hit” for the franchise, however.



“If you know him ... he’s not here for a sugar hit. He’ll have a lot to say and a lot of things, and he’ll steer that direction pretty well,” Mather said. “He’s got some fairly firm beliefs, in how the game is played and what success looks like, and that’s what we really want from him. “It [the Waratahs environment] will have some direction, that’s for sure. He’s very clear on how he wants things done, and it might be a bit of a wake-up call for some of us in terms of how we do things. That track record of success buys you that ability to do that.” Cheika’s coaching staff is yet to be finalised, but former 2014 Waratah back-rower Wycliff Palu is a chance to also return as an assistant. Tom Carter, Locky McCaffrey and Dan Palmer are on the existing staff and on contract for next year, but Mather said the reality is that some change is likely. Cheika’s exit from the Wallabies in 2019 was acrimonious, and he conceded later he had poor relationships with then chief executive Raelene Castle and chairman Cameron Clyne. Waugh was on the RA board at the time, but Mather said none of that history was a problem during negotiations seven years later.



“They say time heals all wounds – it’s a long time ago when he left and there’s a lot of water under the bridge. So when his name came up in conversations, there were never any sort of major obstacles raised as a red flag not to have that conversation and see if he was interested and vice versa from Cheik,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Super Rugby Back in blue: Cheika set to return as Waratahs coach A believer in there can only be one boss, Cheika said in 2020 he “should have quit” when Scott Johnson was appointed above him as director of rugby above him in 2019. Asked if he believed Cheika could work within an organisational structure of RA sitting above the Waratahs as owners, Mather said: “All head coaches want full control, don’t they? But like most things, there’s always limits to what that full control actually looks like. We’re working within a structure with RA and Michael knows exactly what he’s coming into.” Cheika is not the only 2014 Waratah returning, with Bernard Foley and Nick Phipps having also signed for a season in 2027. Roosters back-rower Angus Crichton is also coming across to the Waratahs.



Suaalii positional shift flagged in Wallabies squad for Argentina Coach Les Kiss has flagged a potential move for Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii into the Wallabies’ back three after the NSW superstar was cleared to return from a hamstring injury for the two-Test tour of Argentina. Kiss released a largely unchanged Wallabies squad on Wednesday for the series with the Pumas, which will see them clash in San Salvador de Jujuy on August 30 and Mendoza on September 6. Loading The two major additions from the Wallabies squads that downed Japan in Osaka and Townsville were Len Ikitau, who missed both games with an ankle injury, and Suaalii, who was out from the big win at the weekend in Townsville with a hamstring problem.



In an interesting twist, however, one of the men who dropped out the squad to make room for the star duo was fullback Jock Campbell, just a few days after the 31-year-old was named as Queensland’s best player. Campbell started for the Wallabies in the first Test of the year against Ireland before being contentiously moved to the bench for the Test against France in Brisbane, where he was used as a five-eighth. Campbell has since not featured for the Wallabies. After coming in for Suaalii in Townsville, Josh Flook also dropped out of the squad, but Kiss has not made room for Ikitau and Suaalii by dropping any other of his centres; namely Hunter Paisami and Isaac Henry. Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii celebrate after Max Jorgensen’s winning try in 2024. AP Both turned in outstanding performances for the Wallabies as a starting midfield in Townsville, with Henry playing strongly at No.13 in his run-on debut.



His form prompted questions post-game about whether Suaalii might be looked at as a winger or fullback. The omission of Campbell suggests Kiss may be considering that for the Argentina trip. Kiss moved Suaalii to wing in Osaka when Henry entered the game in the second half. Tom Wright is the starting fullback, but with Campbell gone, the back-up would be between Max Jorgensen, Suaalii and Ben Donaldson. In other news, Tom Hooper has also been named in the squad, and as forecast, Taniela Tupou will also tour Argentina. The pair play for overseas clubs but are remaining with the Wallabies under World Rugby’s regulation 9. The rule allows the mandatory release of players by clubs for Test rugby.



With one more game of a suspension to serve, Miles Amatosero was also left out. Kiss said in statement: “As coaches we’ve looked to maintain consistency in selection with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks, through their hard work and connection on and off the field. “Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it’s one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Construction boss accused of plotting standover in secret sushi shop meeting with bikies
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Construction boss accused of plotting standover in secret sushi shop meeting with bikies Nick McKenzie Updated August 19, 2026 — 5:26pm ,first published 11:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A senior executive of Australian infrastructure giant BMD has been accused of secretly meeting violent members of a Melbourne bikie gang in a Brisbane sushi restaurant as part of a plot to threaten a CFMEU activist blamed for causing problems on an Albanese government-funded project. The revelations have prompted the Labor-backed CFMEU administrator, Michael Crosby, to issue a fresh call for government action to combat the “complete failure of the regulatory system” and to call on companies with alleged links to bikie gangs and the underworld to clean up their backyards. BMD manager Robert Pickard has also been accused in a Queensland inquiry of attempting to cover up the incident after the CFMEU crane driver complained that the leader of a three-man Melbourne bikie crew had threatened to burn down his house and murder his family during a subsequent confrontation on the $350 million Centenary Bridge project. Counsel assisting the Queensland Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU, Eddy Gisonda, KC, suggested on Wednesday afternoon that the terrifying standover incident occurred a short time after Pickard had met the bikie trio at a sushi shop a short stroll from the bridge redevelopment.



Related Article Building Bad ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies But while being questioned by Gisonda, Pickard repeatedly denied allegations that he knew of or witnessed the alleged Comanchero gang standover on June 5, 2024. He also dismissed suggestions he had met the bikies at the sushi shop or coordinated the alleged standover with the owner of BMD’s security subcontractor, Melbourne company Host. Pickard’s denials came after Gisonda presented a detailed circumstantial case to back up his accusation that Pickard and BMD’s human resources chief, Steve Thomas, appeared to have played a key role in the suspected Comanchero standover of CFMEU-affiliated crane driver Cody Raymond, a man blamed for helping the construction union target BMD. Evidence aired by Gisonda before Commissioner Stuart Wood included receipts showing that one of the three bikies had purchased sushi just minutes after Pickard and Thomas had placed orders at the sushi shop. A short time after that, Pickard and Thomas can be seen on CCTV walking towards the Centenary Bridge project as they are trailed by three Comancheros and Melbourne businessman Gary Samuel, the BMD security subcontractor who was hired to counter an aggressive campaign by the CFMEU targeting BMD.



Pickard disagreed with Gisonda’s suggestion that he and Thomas had led the bikies to the work site at a distance to “to make sure the coast was clear” before Raymond was approached and threatened. Phone data presented by Gisonda also revealed repeated contact or attempted contact between Samuel and both Pickard and Thomas around the time Samuel was picking up the three Melbourne bikies from Brisbane airport, as well as just after what the barrister alleged was a secret rendezvous at the sushi outlet. During the hearing, Wood appeared to accept that Samuel had engineered the bikie standover in retaliation for the conduct of the CFMEU. “It makes sense for Mr Samuel to do this,” Wood suggested, referring to the use of the three feared bikie identities.



“It might be quite unlawful ... [but he had been] taking a knife to a gun fight and he wants to improve the tactics” in respect of BMD’s strategy, he said, to resist CFMEU pressure and in light of the indifference of state authorities to union conduct. “I am not saying it excuses him … But it gives a rational explanation for what he did,” Wood said of Samuel. Rob Pickard (right), General Manager, Queensland and Northern Territory, BMD Constructions is seen being questioned by Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC (left) during the Commission of Inquiry. AAPIMAGE During the hearing, Wood also queried why BMD had told police in November 2024 that CCTV of the bikie incident was no longer available, given the company had provided the vision to Wood’s commission earlier this year. Wood also asked Gisonda to make inquiries about whether it was unlawful for a company or person to “deliberately or inadvertently mislead the police”. But Pickard dismissed the claim that he or BMD were party to a bikie threat plot or that Pickard had sought to “deflect” attention away from his own or Samuel’s role in allegedly coordinating the potentially criminal act.



Wednesday’s hearing will ultimately inform Wood as he weighs whether the circumstantial evidence gathered by Gisonda and the Queensland Police investigators assisting his inquiry is strong enough to allow Wood to make an adverse finding about Pickard or BMD’s involvement in the bikie plot. Gisonda opened the hearing on Wednesday by revealing that law enforcement agencies suspected the Comancheros of seeking to build a construction empire via front companies and by infiltrating union ranks. Queensland’s Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU has laid bare the involvement of the Comancheros in the construction industry. Getty Images He claimed police intelligence, including extensive phone data, indicated the Comanchero bikie gang had in early 2024 embarked on a concerted effort to do this in both Victoria and Queensland. According to Gisonda, this effort involved the now former Melbourne-based Comanchero boss Bemir Saracevic. Saracevic is the same bikie figure Gisonda identified as allegedly leading the standover of Raymond.



Gisonda also tabled union-backed enterprise bargaining agreements allegedly secured by Comanchero-linked building firms in Victoria, including an EBA signed off by the CFMEU administration last month and by the Australian Workers’ Union in 2025. A separate investigation by The Age has established that basic due diligence should have revealed to both unions that these firms had business links to the Comancheros: one had previously been refused a licence to operate by Victoria’s Labour Hire Authority, while both had clear links to the wife of Saracevic. Bemir Saracevic. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU In a statement, Crosby told this masthead that the EBA his union had recently granted a firm now alleged to be Comanchero-linked was intended to protect workers. The CFMEU administrator said it was up to government, and not the CFMEU, to prevent underworld infiltration. “The Administrator has called for a Fit and Proper Persons Test to be applied to participants in the construction industry. It’s time the industry was cleaned up. It’s time to stop blaming workers for the complete failure of the regulatory system. It’s not the job of the union to clean up the industry,” he said.



“We’ll clean up our backyard – it’s time for employers to clean up theirs.” Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad ‘Idiots in Victoria’ holding back CFMEU: Administrator blasts former union bosses, demands reform The Queensland hearing has also placed immense scrutiny on BMD, which is currently working on Victoria’s Eastern Freeway upgrade and other Big Build projects. In Sydney, it is working on the new international airport in Western Sydney. In July, the Crisafulli government in Queensland announced that BMD had won the contract to undertake early works for the new Brisbane Stadium Olympics venue. Asked by this masthead about the evidence heard at the commission suggesting BMD associated with underworld-linked figures in the alleged Centenary Bridge stand-over incident and whether BMD’s internal investigation into the matter was adequate, the company’s spokesperson said: “BMD has additional representatives to appear over the coming days and it would be premature for us to comment.”



When Thomas, BMD’s human resources chief, gave evidence to the commission on Wednesday afternoon, he also denied being aware of the three bikie figures as they and Samuel appeared to trail Pickard and the human resources manager as they walked towards the location where Raymond was confronted. Thomas insisted he had not witnessed or had any prior knowledge of the bikie gang activity on June 5. Thomas, who will give further evidence on Thursday, also defended his failure to provide CCTV of the incident to the QLD Police when they first sought it in late 2024. “I took all reasonable steps to locate that footage at that time… I wasn’t able to locate that footage,” Thomas said. The revelations at the Queensland inquiry give Australians a taste of what is likely to be unveiled at the promised and upcoming Victorian royal commission. Many of the key subjects discussed at this week’s hearings in Brisbane are from Melbourne and are variously entrenched in both Victoria’s underworld and its building sector. SportRacingHorse racing Clark hopeful for third Rowley Mile win on Punch Lane August 19, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jockey Tim Clark will be out to make it a third Listed Pioneer Services Rowley Mile (1600m) in recent years when partnering the Anthony and Sam Freedman-trained Punch Lane in Thursday’s $200,000 feature. Clark won the event on Gaulois in 2019 and Arbeitsam in 2017, and has high hopes that Punch Lane can repeat the dose. Jockey Tim Clark. Getty Images “It profiles as a nice race for him,” said Clark, who has been aboard Punch Lane in trackwork. “He likes getting his toe in the ground so the prospect of a rain-affected track is in his favour.



“The mile suits and from the wide draw there’s a good straight run to try and get a spot.” Punch Lane was a last-start fourth in the Winter Challenge at Rosehill behind Midnight Dynamite, which Clark will ride in Saturday’s Group 1 Winx Stakes at Randwick. “It was a good run by Punch Lane in that event,” Clark said. “He held on pretty well and he’s had a trial since so he’s ready to go.” Clark will combine with the Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott-prepared Tempestuous when it resumes from a lengthy spell in the Peter Smith Memorial Super Maiden Plate (1100m).



“He was off the scene for a long time after showing ability as a two-year-old,” said Clark. Related Article Horse racing Race-by-race preview and tips for Hawkesbury on Thursday “He’s had three recent trials in preparation for his return and has been a bit hit-and-miss at the start, so I’m hoping he can put it all together at Hawkesbury.” The mount on the Gerald Ryan- and Sterling Alexiou-trained Esquire awaits Clark in the Happy Retirement Adam Carney Maiden Plate (1300m). “He ran well on debut when finishing second to Steel Will,” Clark said.



“Steel Will made the form look good when winning at Rosehill last Saturday.” Clark has two other rides at Hawkesbury with both being for trainer Sara Ryan. He will steer Master Zous in the Micway Midway Class 1 Handicap (1100m) and Galactic Force in the Brad Widdup Champion Trainer 2025-2026 Champion Local Trainer Benchmark 64 Handicap (1300m).
