World.title: Health minister agrees to investigation into beleaguered Concord hospital
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWDoctors at work Health minister agrees to investigation into beleaguered Concord hospital Rachel Rasker August 19, 2026 — 4:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NSW Auditor-General’s office will investigate allegations of targeted disciplinary action within Sydney Local Health District in what appears to be a last-ditch effort to fend off a mutiny among Concord Hospital staff. Health Minister Ryan Park agreed to the probe one day before senior doctors in the hospital’s Medical Staff Council (MSC) were due to hold a vote of no confidence in NSW Health leadership and demand a parliamentary inquiry into the NSW health ministry. Dr Raoul Pope was disciplined by NSW Health following social media posts. Wolter Peeters The doctors’ demands, fuelled by the suspension of outspoken spinal neurosurgeon Dr Raoul Pope, threatened to spark a statewide revolt among public hospital clinicians fed up with alleged widespread governance failures and a lack of accountability within NSW Health. In an email sent to members of the MSC on Wednesday and seen by the Herald, former chair Dr Winston Cheung said Minister Park agreed to an investigation into the disciplinary processes at Concord.



Related Article Doctors at work Sydney doctors plan revolt against NSW Health “We have been asking for an independent, external investigation into aspects of governance for four years, and finally this request has been actioned,” the email read. “The scope of the investigation will be determined by the NSW Auditor-General without interference by the government or NSW Health.” Cheung said he expected the investigation would examine any allegations of a “weaponisation” of policy to discipline staff who have raised concerns. Cheung’s email counselled that the vote of no confidence should not proceed on Thursday. In July, this masthead revealed that Pope had received a disciplinary letter from the hospital’s people and culture team about his emails and LinkedIn activity, which were critical of hospital management.



Pope was told his actions were “undermining staff confidence in leadership” and “inconsistent with your obligations to protect the reputation and interests of SLHD and NSW Health”. Following the Herald’s article, Pope was suspended without pay from his role as visiting medical officer at Concord. The disciplinary action was “a risk management measure” due to “risks to staff or patient health, safety or welfare”, the people and culture team advised in an internal memo seen by the Herald. An Instagram video of Greens health spokesperson Dr Amanda Cohn sharing the news of the Pope’s suspension in parliament amassed more than 300,000 views this month and was widely circulated among clinicians, adding pressure on the government.



“Why do essential frontline health workers continue to be punished by this government for their advocacy for better health services?” Cohn said in the clip. In a statement, Cohn said the Auditor-General’s investigation was an “important acknowledgement of the seriousness of the issues that frontline staff have been raising, and a valuable next step”. Senior doctors at Concord Hospital have raised concerns about what they call widespread workplace issues. James Brickwood Cohn said she would still pursue a wider parliamentary inquiry. “Health care workers must feel safe and supported to be able to raise issues about their workplace and patients’ safety,” she said.



Related Article Healthcare Delayed cancer diagnoses, broken bones missed: The patients caught up in a Sydney hospital fail “Suppression of their voices by NSW Health is not an isolated or local issue [to Concord], and I am optimistic that a parliamentary inquiry will be able to examine this broader problem.” In Cheung’s email to doctors, he said he hoped the staff who had “resigned or who have suffered will finally get justice and closure”. He called the meeting with Park “very constructive” and said the group – which also included the MSC chairs of Canterbury Hospital and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital – discussed issues including resourcing, staffing and the social media policy. Both the doctors’ union and opposition MPs have criticised the social media policy, introduced by NSW Health in November last year.



When questioned in a budget estimates hearing on Wednesday, Fatima Abbas, the deputy secretary of people, culture and governance at NSW Health, said the policy was not designed to suppress freedom of communication. “The intent is not to discourage appropriate discourse or discussions about issues,” she said. Abbas could not answer how many clinicians had been suspended under the policy, as she said the information was not collected centrally. In his email, Cheung said he looked forward to “the truth-telling that this investigation will allow”. “We should wait for the terms of reference for the investigation from the Auditor-General before making any further decisions on this matter, but I expect this engagement from them will only be positive,” it read. Park and the Sydney Local Health District have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Arthur's Pass camp site torn up by 4WD vehicles
World.content:
The Department of Conservation (DOC) is appealing to the public for help after a popular camp site at Arthur's Pass in the South Island was torn up by 4WD vehicles.

The popular and picturesque Klondyke Corner Campsite draws thousands of visitors each year and was a key feature of the annual Coast to Coast multi-sport race.

Aerial photos illustrate the extend of damage which was believed to have happened on 1 August at about 4pm.

An aerial view of damage from four-wheel drive vehicles at Klondyke Corner Campsite in Arthur's Pass. Supplied / Department of Conservation

DOC operations manager Leeann Ellis said it was incredibly disappointing.

"The vehicles have left deep tyre tracks over a large area, compacting the soil, creating wide ruts and making the site much more susceptible to erosion in heavy rain," she said.

"They have also destroyed plants and opened the area up for weeds to grow and take over. Its ruined what was a fantastic place and created the potential for a muddy mess in heavy rain."

The department was working with police to try and identify the vehicles and said it welcomed any information from the public.

An aerial view of damage from four-wheel drive vehicles at Klondyke Corner Campsite in Arthur's Pass. Supplied / Department of Conservation

It was illegal to damage any national park's natural or historic features and to drive vehicles on off-formed roads.

Offenders can face heavy penalties, including infringement fines and prosecution.

Under the National Parks Act, interfering with or damaging a historic feature in a national park carried a maximum penalty for an individual of up to one year in prison, a $100,000 fine, or both.

"We appreciate four-wheel driving is an increasingly popular recreational activity," Ellis said.

"There are some fantastic tracks where drivers can challenge their skills and access some beautiful locations like the Edwards Valley and Maling Pass 4WD tracks in the St James Conservation Area. Our plea is don't go off road and cause damage to areas which are protected for a reason.

World.title: Urgent debate or urgent farewell: MPs discuss Chris Penk
World.content:
Tuesday's urgent parliamentary debate on Chris Penk's demotion was about a fairly specific topic: the prime minister's decision to remove one of his ministers from Cabinet for disloyalty. In practice, it was a rather more eclectic collection of reckons from around the House. At times it resembled a fond farewell tribute.

Urgent debate or urgent farewell: MPs debate demotion of Chris Penk The House Download MP3 5m

There was the expected political crossfire over the events of the previous week. Labour argued it exposed deeper problems for Christopher Luxon's leadership. National MPs' responses were tantamount to "nothing to see here", instead aiming to spotlight Labour's hypothetical tax policies. But there were also more personal interpretations of the situation.

ACT's Simon Court used a decent portion of his contribution to lament the end of Penk's ministerial tenure, and praise Penk's work in the Building and Construction portfolio. He tucked in some campaigning too. Court is standing in Penk's electorate and hoping some of Penk's supporters might jump into the ACT waka instead of the National one as a protest or proxy vote.

Simon Court praises Chris Penk and then makes a plea for voters to choose him as Penk's replacement during an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk. VNP / Phil Smith

Court's praise contrasted with the political argument surrounding Penk's removal. At times the debate sounded less like a dispute over a ministerial decision and more like a valedictory for someone who had already left.

Te Pāti Māori's Debbie Ngarewa-Packer and Labour's Carmel Sepuloni both went out of their way to acknowledge the now former minister personally, describing him in warm terms as an "honourable man" who was "here for the right reasons", and praising the way he conducted himself across the House.

Te Pāti Māori leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer during an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge. VNP / Phil Smith

Te Pāti Māori's Debbie Ngarewa-Packer described Penk as "one of the better human beings on that side".

Former National Party leader Judith Collins appears to enjoy an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge. VNP / Phil Smith

Almost the only party not to praise the fallen minister was his own party. As speeches ping-ponged back and forth between the two major parties, the very short contributions from National MPs largely stuck to the party line: Penk acted alone, actions have consequences, and it was time to move on.

Then there was Kieran McAnulty, who praised Penk but focused on picking apart attempts by various National MPs to draw a line under the events.

Kieran McAnulty dissects the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge. VNP / Phil Smith

Through all of this, there were two notable absences - both the demoter and the demoted.

Christopher Luxon's seat remains empty during an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge against him. VNP / Phil Smith

Chris Penk isn't at Parliament this week, and was not in the House to explain his actions, or respond to the various assessments of his character and political judgment. The prime minister had departed the House prior to the end of Question Time; his actions as well as Penk's were debated without him. The one minister present who was discussed was Erica Stanford, who sat still and silent, like a pupil sent to await the headmaster.

Ultimately, the House's traversal of last week's political melodrama was a forum for criticism, defence, campaigning and a fond farewell from the most unexpected quarters, missing only its protagonists.

You can listen to the audio version of this story, by clicking the link near the top of the page.

World.title: Damning report into fatal Mount Maunganui landslide shows tragedy was preventable
World.content:
Landslide risk at Mount Maunganui was found decades before fatal accident Checkpoint Download MP3 12m

A report into the fatal landslide at Mount Maunganui says information identifying a risk to life was received, filed, discussed, forwarded - and then left.

"The failure was not the fault of any one person; it was the failure of a system that enabled an identified risk to life to remain unowned, un-escalated and unmanaged," the report said.

Six people died in the landslide on 22 January 2026. They were Lisa Maclennan, Susan Knowles, Jacqualine Wheeler, Måns Loke Bernhardsson, Sharon Maccanico, and Max Furse-Kee.

The six victims of the Mt Maunganui landslide - Måns Loke Bernhardsson, 20, Lisa Maclennan, 50, Susan Knowles, 71, Sharon Maccanico, 15, Max Furse-Kee, 15, and Jacqualine Wheeler, 71. Supplied

The external review was commissioned by the Tauranga City Council in early February.

Retired high court judge Hon Paul Davison KSO KC, who wrote the report, said they had come to Mauao to do what thousands of New Zealanders do each summer - to camp in a spectacular setting beside the ocean beach and beneath a mountain of great beauty and cultural significance.

They trusted they would be safe and if any natural hazard risk arose, that they would be warned and protected.

"Nothing in this report should be allowed to obscure that," Davison said.

Watch the release of the findings below:

"The central conclusion of this review is sobering in its simplicity. This was not a hazard that was unknown, hidden, or beyond the reach of foresight.

"For more than two decades, one competent consultant after another identified the landslide hazard to the campground, located it on the very slope that failed, and explained - sometimes in stark terms - what the consequences of a landslide occurring could be.

"As long ago as 1999, Dr Laurie Richards warned that the siting of fragile holiday accommodation directly beneath these slopes was imprudent and that the risk to sleeping occupants was high."

The slip at Mauao, Mount Maunganui as seen from the air. Screengrab / Amy Till

He said in 2006 it went further, estimating that a debris flow of the kind that had happened before would place some 30 people in its path and kill 21.

The same warning and the same precisely-marked aerial photograph of the historic scarp was repeated "again and again" over the years that followed.

"And experience had repeatedly demonstrated that high levels of extended rainfall increased the likelihood of landslips occurring, and extremely high levels of extended heavy rainfall increased the risk of large scale landslides occurring."

Davison said in late 2023 and again in mid 2025, a Trigger Action Response Plan - which was an effective means of mitigating the risk - was recommended and not acted on.

"The knowledge was there. The means of reducing the risk of a landslide occurring was identified, available and relatively inexpensive to implement."

Floral tribute to the victims of the landslide. CHARLOTTE COOK / RNZ

He concluded that what was missing, was not knowledge, but an organisation able to hold, assess, and act on it.

"The geohazard sat at the administrative and legal boundary that exists between the mountain and the campground, and responsibility for landslide risk fell somewhere between the Tauranga City Council teams responsible for each."

Davison said no single person within the TCC organisation "owned it" and no system mandatorily required the risk to be recorded, escalated, or tracked.

"Reports identifying a risk to life were received, filed, discussed, forwarded - and then left."

Nick Monro

He said successive restructures dispersed the people who held the institutional memory and continuity of that invaluable knowledge was treated as expendable.

"Time and time again the recommended measures or controls were scoped out or simply not actioned."

Davison said on the morning of 22 January, these systematic flaws combined and were compounded.

"Warnings came early and from several directions."

This included from the intense rainfall, from the large slips already coming down around the mountain, from several smaller slips on the slope, and from muddy water streaming from the foot of the slope before it finally failed.

"The instinct to move people away from the toe of the slope was even voiced by some of those who observed these signs, but there was no plan against which to assess those warnings, no threshold criteria requiring action, and no training of staff enabling them to recognise observable signs which indicated an elevated risk of slope failure and no one charged with making a properly informed evacuation decision.

"The most consequential safety decision of that morning was left, by default, to the manager at the campground who have been given neither the tools nor the knowledge to make it.

"In my view, the criticism justly and appropriately lies with the organisation that left the campground manager and his staff so ill-equipped and unprepared to make the decisions that could have avoided this tragedy."

Tauranga mayor Mahé Drysdale speaks at a vigil a week after the landslide. Hayden Woodward

He said had a Trigger Action Response Plan of the kind been twice recommended, that morning would have looked very different.

"Such a plan would not have depended on anyone reading the slope correctly in the moment. Its rainfall trigger would likely have been engaged overnight, by rainfall that was the heaviest in some 20 years; and if not, independently by its second trigger - the prolific and very obvious discharge of muddy water from the toe of the slope, observable for several hours before the eventual slope failure - should have required the same response."

He said each trigger on their own would have called for at least the precautionary evacuation and exclusion of the campsites.

"Had those areas been evacuated and kept clear, as such a plan would have required, the people who lost their lives would not have been within the path of the landslide when the slope failed.

"The loss of life could have in all likelihood been averted."

Davison said it was important to be clear that the review did not find that any individual did anything intentionally wrong, or that any one or more persons' acts or omissions caused these deaths.

He also did not find that the removal of trees in 2019 caused the landslide and makes no findings as to civil, criminal, or disciplinary liability.

Emergency Management Minister reacts to Mount landslide report Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

What it did find, he said, was that the tragedy was preventable.

"I do not mean by that that anyone could have known that this slope would fail at this moment, on this particular morning - no one could.

"I mean something more deeply troubling; that the hazard was known, that an effective and inexpensive means of managing the risk it posed had twice been recommended, and that the council had every opportunity to put it in place.

"What was required was not extraordinary foresight."

Davison said the recommendations he's made are directed to building a single accountable ownership of every risk to life.

"Mauao is a revered taonga, a sacred maunga, a place of belonging, of healing, and of inspiration for the people of Tauranga Moana, and for many people privileged to visit it and who hold and treat it with respect.

"It will always be so. But the events of 22 January 2026 have shown, at the most heartbreaking cost, that reverence for the mountain and responsibility for those who climb it or gather at its foot must go hand in hand.

"While the law draws a boundary between the reserve and the campground, the mountain recognises no such line, and neither does the landslide risk that lies within its slopes."

He said if the recommendations are acted upon, it will materially reduce the chance of such a tragedy ever occurring again.

Speaking after the report's release, police said the investigation into the landslide was ongoing.

"We are also continuing to make enquiries on behalf of the Coroner. Police's Family Liaison Officers remain in contact with the families, and our heartfelt thoughts are with those who lost their loved ones," Detective Inspector Lindsay Pilbrow, Bay of Plenty Crime Manager, said in a statement.

'Weighs heavily in our hearts and on our shoulders'

Tauranga City Council chief executive Matty Grenfell is adamant he won't be stepping down following the review and says it was a failure of the system, not one person.

Grenfell, who has led the organisation for the past eight years, told Checkpoint he hasn't offered his resignation.

"My focus is on leading the organisation through what is going to be a difficult period. This is the first of three other reviews that are happening.

"It needs stability, it needs someone who knows the organisation, it needs someone who can effect these changes."

Gernfell said he was the best person to lead the implementation of the report's recommendations.

Current and former staff are haunted by the missed opportunities to prevent the loss of six lives, he said.

"There are many of us in council carrying the weight of this event and it weighs heavily in our hearts and on our shoulders.

"I'm sure every staff member who was involved directly or indirectly have been playing back the morning of the 22nd of January and thinking, 'What could we, what should we have done?'"

World.title: Govt inquiry into fatal landslides 'will reach its own conclusions' - chair
World.content:
The government's inquiry into the deadly Mauao landslide will consider the council's conclusions, but will reach its "own conclusions and recommendations in due course", says the inquiry chair.

The Tauranga City Council today released details of its external review into the landslide on 22 January that claimed the lives of Lisa Maclennan, Susan Knowles, Jacqualine Wheeler, Måns Loke Bernhardsson, Sharon Maccanico, and Max Furse-Kee.

The six victims of the Mt Maunganui landslide - Måns Loke Bernhardsson, 20, Lisa Maclennan, 50, Susan Knowles, 71, Sharon Maccanico, 15, Max Furse-Kee, 15, and Jacqualine Wheeler, 71. Supplied

The council report by retired high court judge Hon Paul Davison KSO KC found nothing was done after information identifying a risk to life was received, filed, discussed and forwarded.

"The failure was not the fault of any one person; it was the failure of a system that enabled an identified risk to life to remain unowned, un-escalated and unmanaged," the report said.

The government is conducting its own inquiry into the landslide, as well as a second fatal landslide which occurred in January.

A landslide also fell on to three properties on Welcome Bay Road in Pāpāmoa, killing a grandmother and grandchild.

The government is also looking at the Pāpāmoa slip which claimed the lives of Austen Keith Richardson and his grandmother Yao Fang. Supplied / Police

Inquiry chair Sir Mark O'Regan said it would consider Davison's review alongside other evidence gathered.

"The government inquiry's scope covers both the Mauao and Welcome Bay Road landslides, and the actions of all relevant agencies, not just Tauranga City Council.

"The council's review and the government Inquiry are independent processes, each with their own terms of reference. Although the inquiry must consider the Davison review, it will reach its own conclusions and recommendations in due course.

"Our sincere sympathy remains with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, those who were injured, and everyone affected by January's landslides."

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said the government would consider the findings of the review alongside the government's inquiry.

"My thoughts are with the victims of the January landslides, their families and loved ones, and the emergency services personnel and community members who responded during an incredibly difficult time," Watts said.

"I'll be looking through the detailed report and its recommendations, as will local government and emergency management authorities. At first glance, as Mayor Drysdale has said, the findings are deeply confronting."

He said the council accepting the findings was "a good first step" and the government's focus remained on ensuring "all relevant facts are examined, lessons are identified, and recommendations are developed to help prevent similar tragedies from occurring in the future".

Public submissions to the government's inquiry have been extended to 4 September, with a final report expected in December.

Emergency Response Minister Mark Mitchell said he had not read the report yet but was "aware that the findings are not flash".

"I had some members of the family reach out to me about two weeks ago, and I had a long chat with them. They've just been briefed on it. I'm not going to comment on what their comments are because I'll allow them to do that.

"I'm a huge believer in accountability... it's shocking to me that we lost six people on the Mount and two at Welcome Bay... I've been right alongside the families literally from that morning, and it's been incredibly tough for the families, for the community, for the whole country.

"I've only just received the report, so I need time to go over it myself ... we'll have to wait and see what the government inquiry contains but I would say that there's probably some of the information will be in both reports, without a doubt.

"I'm looking for lessons learnt, whether it be the report that comes back to council or any report that comes across my desk."

NZ Police Bay of Plenty crime manager Inspector Lindsay Pilbrow said they were investigating both landslides and making enquiries on behalf of the coroner.

"Police's Family Liaison Officers remain in contact with the families, and our heartfelt thoughts are with those who lost their loved ones.

World.title: Actions of Mount Maunganui landslide victim Lisa Maclennan, who helped save the lives of others, detailed in report
World.content:
The actions of Lisa Maclennan, a victim of January's deadly Mount Maunganui landslide who was hailed as a hero, have been laid bare in a damning report into what took place that day.

Six people died in the landslide on 22 January 2026. They were Lisa Maclennan, Susan Knowles, Jacqualine Wheeler, Måns Loke Bernhardsson, Sharon Maccanico, and Max Furse-Kee.

Maclennan, 51, was earlier hailed as a hero by a woman at the campground who said Maclennan had woken her up shortly before 5am to warn her a slip had pushed her campervan forward.

Lisa Maclennan was one of the six people killed in a landslide at Mount Maunganui in January. NZ POLICE / SUPPLIED

Wednesday's report further detailed the actions Maclennan and her husband Travis took that morning to try and contact staff at the campground about their concerns of further slips.

Travis Maclennan told the report it had been a spur of the moment decision to go to the Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday park and they were given a site for their campervan directly adjacent to the foot of the slop of the mountain.

About 4.30am on January 22, Lisa Maclennan was awoken by the movement of the caravan and hearing a noise she woke her husband and the pair went outside to see the slope behind the campervan had come down and hit the rear of the vehicle.

They moved their campervan and Lisa Maclennan woke the occupants of a small blue tent pitched beside them as she worried the man and his young daughter could be trapped if any more of the slope failed.

Tributes at the cordon of the deadly lanslide in January. RNZ / Lauren Crimp

The couple wanted to urgently get hold of the campground's management so other campers could be alerted ot the risk. But multiple attempts to reach them by phone over the next few hours were unsuccessful.

The pair also tried using the intercom at the campground and knocked on walls of the building to attract attention from anyone inside but received no response.

About 5.15am they noticed another slip had come down further along the driveway and they woke up the occupants of two cabins and a campervan nearby.

Until 7am they went between visiting the office and trying to get in touch with management and standing by their campervan talking to other campers.

The pair also took photographs of the slips as the light improved.

When a council worker, whose name was redacted by the report, arrived at the campground shortly after 7am, Lisa Maclennan told them they had been trying to contact staff. The worker described her as "frustrated and agitated" because she could not get hold of anyone.

Travis Maclennan said they later saw a man with a campground shirt who they asked to come to their side of the campground to see the slips.

He said the worker had "showed no interest" in what Lisa Maclennan was saying and responded in a "dismissive way" saying he would "get there when he got there".

Lisa Maclennan helped warn others of the risk of further slips. Supplied / Givealittle

The worker, whose name was redacted, disputed that wording and told the report he said he would go over as soon as he was finished.

By 7.40am Lisa Maclennan was warning people near the amenities block of potential further slips, the report said.

Two campground staff members also looked at the slip the couple identified.

Shortly after 8.30am, the couple decided to leave the campground - the storm had passed and the sun was out. They decided to shower before leaving as the weather had cleared.

Travis Maclennan went first and was waiting by the campervan while Lisa Maclennan went to have her shower shortly before the slope failed without any visible warning just before 9.30am.

Officials work at the scene of the landslide. Alan Gibson / Gibson Images Ltd

Lisa Maclennan's body was found five days after the slip. She was identified with the help of DNA, dental records and a butterfly tattoo above her ankle.

A statement released on Wednesday by her husband Travis Maclenan, said the report highlighted her "extraordinary and selfless actions" on the morning of the landslide.

World.title: Gisborne slash clash: Mayor feels like 'meat in the middle'
World.content:
Gisborne Mayor Rehette Stoltz says she feels like the ''meat in the middle'' between her community and the forestry sector.

Forestry Minister Todd McClay had told the Gisborne District Council that its approach to sediment management and forestry slash was too tough and a facilitator had been appointed to help "reset the relationship" with the sector.

Stoltz told Checkpoint that a meeting with the minister on Wednesday had been "productive" and the Gisborne community deserved a "collaborative" approach between local and central government.

Gisborne mayor meets with Forestry minister over approach to 'slash' Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

She said community members told her that the council's approach to consent was not tough enough, but that the forestry industry had expressed a different view.

"We are getting constant feedback that it is strict, or that the industry is finding that the consent conditions are stricter than what they would expect, so, what we then said is 'We are doing our work, but we hear you'. So we are going to ask an independent panel to evaluate what we have in our consenting regime, how we plan and is it proportionate to the risk we are trying to look after?"

Stoltz said the council had appointed an independent reviewer - Chris Finlayson - to look at its consent conditions.

"I feel sometimes like the meat in the middle, where we are trying to look after our environment, we are trying to make sure there is economic activity as well. So, from one side we are hearing 'it feels like this is too tough'. Our community are feeding back to us saying ít's not tough enough. So we are testing that, because at the end of the day we do want to make sure it is fit for purpose and that's exactly what we are doing now."

Stoltz said following Cyclone Gabrielle the government appointed a panel to investigate the impact of storm damage caused by wood debris and sediment on communities.

World.title: Winter illnesses harming students' education, NZPF president says
World.content:
The principal of a Napier kura says more than half of their students are not at school this week because they are sick.

Maraenui Bilingual School Tumuaki, Traci Liddall, said 67 percent of their 125 students stayed home on Monday, and 56 percent did on Tuesday and Wednesday. All but two of those students were reported to have flu-like symptoms.

Data from the Ministry of Education showed almost 10 percent of class time was lost across the country last week due to illness. The past couple of weeks have been the worst in three years for school absences due to illness and medical reasons.

Hawke's Bay has been hit hard - one day last week, Napier Girl's High had 20 percent of its students, or about 200 girls, off due to sickness. The Terrace School - a primary in Waikpukurau - had 76 kids off on Tuesday, about a third of its roll, as well as six teachers.

Liddall said the Ministry of Education advising parents to send children to school with mild symptoms like a runny nose was unhelpful.

"It bothers me that the ministry are on our back about attendance, but we can't help this.

"As much as we would like the tamariki to be at kura, I'd rather sick kids stay at home and get properly well before they come to school, otherwise they just spread germs.

"Sending kids with sniffles is not a good message to be sending, so I'm disappointed to see that."

She said three teachers at the bilingual school, including herself, were also sick.

They had merged some classes, but they often did that due to small class numbers, to give teachers relief time.

Liddal said she had not seen sickness-related absences this high in her 30-year teaching career, other than during Covid-19.

"Fifteen to 20 percent would be a bad day for absences for us, unless there's something going on in the community, like a big tangi.

"I've never seen anything like this."

Winter illnesses are harming students' education, the president of the New Zealand Principals' Federation says.

Have you been affected by school sickness? Get in touch at iwitness@rnz.co.nz

NZPF president Jason Miles said absences that high affected student learning.

"You've got to work out what the children have missed in that time that they've been away. It's about the teachers knowing their children, knowing what they have missed and looking at what they can do to catch up," he told RNZ.

The principal's federation encouraged children to stay away if they were unwell, but to come back as soon as they were feeling better, he said.

"There are different communities that are hit harder than others for a period of time, and it takes 5-10 days to get over this flu, so in that time you've got a number of children who are sick, a number of children who about to get sick and of course you've got staff who are sick as well."

Illness among staff was particularly problematic, and was putting huge pressure on the relieving teacher pool, particularly in high schools.

"When you've got a lot of children away, it's fairly straightforward, but if you've got more staff away, percentage-wise, than children, then that's a really difficult space for leaders to be in, because that's about getting enough adults to keep your school open.

"So school leaders are either having to double up classes, put management staff in classes, which impacts on other parts of running the school, or rostering some years home."

The Ministry of Education has been approached for comment.

Auckland Primary Principals' Association executive Lucy Naylor told the NZ Herald that parents could not afford to have a "she'll be right attitude" towards illness.

She acknowledged there could be "conflicting messaging" over when to keep children home, however.

Health NZ has official guidance for when children should not be at school.

It states: "If a child is too unwell to learn or they have an infectious illness that could spread easily to others, they need to be kept at home away from school so they can recover or get health advice or care."

World.title: Ikitau back in fray as Wallabies eye Argentina tour
World.content:
Les Kiss has resisted throwing any curveballs ahead of the Wallabies' tour of Argentina, with a fit Len Ikitau the only addition to the squad that produced wins in his first two Tests as coach.

Ikitau (ankle), the 2025 Wallabies player of the year, had minor surgery and missed the recent victories against Japan in Osaka and Townsville.

He has effectively replaced unlucky fullback Jock Campbell, who impressed in the number 15 jersey against Ireland before injuries elsewhere saw him employed as a play-making bench option against France.

With Tom Wright locked in at fullback, Campbell, who was named the Queensland Reds' best player at this week's end-of-season awards, was replaced by Ben Donaldson as the fullback or fly half bench cover for the next three Tests.

Les Kiss seeking pride The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Centre Josh Flook has also been left out while Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii (hamstring) will also return after missing Saturday's Townsville Test, creating a log-jam of midfield options against the world number seven Pumas.

Winger Max Jorgensen has been included despite coming off with a sore chest on Saturday, while code-hopper Zac Lomax remains on the injury list and unavailable for selection.

Lock Miles Amatosero, unavailable for the first Test as part of a three-game suspension for a red card earned in Osaka, was also not considered for selection.

Kiss, who tested new combinations in the pack and centres in his first two games in charge, has otherwise played a straight bat ahead of what will be sterner tests in San Salvador de Jujuy and Mendoza on August 30 and September 6.

"As coaches, we've looked to maintain consistency in selection, with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks through their hard work and connection on and off the field," he said.

"Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it's one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game."

Where Kiss selects Suaalii will be telling after Isaac Henry's strong running and second-phase play at outside centre caught the eye in Townsville.

Hunter Paisami has also impressed at number 12 in Ikitau's absence, leading to questions post-match about where Suaalii fits in the picture.

There is a push for former NRL star Suaalii to move to the wing to ensure more involvement and better harness his aerial ability.

Kiss, who replaced Joe Schmidt ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup, said before his first Test in charge that he was "persisting at number 13 with him at this stage, but I know that he can go to fullback and wing, and that's important to acknowledge as well".

But Campbell and Flook's exclusion from this squad hints that Kiss is now considering a Suaalii switch.

Zane Nonggorr (calf) remains sidelined, with Massimo De Lutiis set for his first full Wallabies tour after arriving late into Osaka and debuting in Townsville.

Wright will notch 50 Test caps if he plays in both Tests.

The squad will assemble in Sydney on Saturday, before departing for Buenos Aires on Sunday.

World.title: Germany star says neurological issue behind two collapses in a week
World.content:
Bayern Munich midfielder Jamal Musiala has revealed a neurological issue but says he is doing well despite collapsing during a preseason game for the second time in a week.

The 23-year-old Germany international went down shortly after entering Wednesday's (AEST) friendly as a substitute in the second half. Players from both teams made a circle around Musiala as he received medical treatment. He was then helped as he walked off the pitch.

Musiala had collapsed Sunday (AEST) during a friendly against Leipzig. German news agency DPA reported he had left the field on his own but still appeared dazed.

After Wednesday's game, Musiala posted a message on his Instagram account, explaining that he had been diagnosed with temporary "but easily treatable absence seizures" caused by a neurological problem.

"These can lead to the moments that happened recently, such as against Leipzig or even now in Heidenheim," Musiala wrote.

Bayern, in its report on Wednesday's game, only said of the incident: "There was a setback when Jamal Musiala had to be subbed off with a knock minutes after coming on."

Jamal Musiala was held up by teammate Ismael Saibari (left) after fainting during Bayern's friendly against RB Leipzig. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

Musiala said he was "very optimistic" and was receiving excellent medical treatment.

"The important thing is that there is no additional health risk," he wrote.

"In close coordination and regular communication with experts, it has been my personal wish to face the challenge and, with the endorsement of the neurological specialists, to devote myself to what helps me most in recovery: to simply live my everyday life and keep up with my passion of playing football," Musiala added.

Bundesliga champion Bayern faces Borussia Dortmund on Sunday AEST in the German Supercup, the traditional curtain-raiser for the season.

AP

World.title: Irankunda says Hanson's monoculture comments upset team during World Cup
World.content:
Socceroos star winger Nestory Irankunda says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's comments on multiculturalism upset many of the players during the recent World Cup.

The Australian team was competing at the tournament in North America in June when Ms Hanson made a speech at the National Press Club saying Australia should end its policy of multiculturalism in favour of a monoculture.

"It really did upset me and it upset a lot of the other boys to see things and hear things like that," Irankunda said.

" I felt a bit emotional but then tried to forget about it. "

Irankunda, who is one of several Socceroos players from a refugee background, told 702 ABC Sydney while he tried to stay off social media it was hard to avoid the senator's comments.

Loading...

"There can be some people who do the wrong thing but that doesn't mean that's all of us," he said.

"There's people like me, and Awer [Mabil], Mohamed Touré that go out there. There's a lot of boys like us that go out there and do the right thing.

"I don't like how they try and put us in the whole same category as the other people who do bad."

Irankunda was born in a refugee camp in Tanzania in 2006 to Burundian parents who fled the nation's civil war. He came to Australia when he was three months old.

Irankunda was speaking with presenter Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney just days after moving from English Championship club Watford to Portuguese side Sporting CP for an undisclosed fee reported to be in the region of $26 million.

The footballer said he probably wouldn't like to speak with the One Nation senator as he was still upset by the comments and "some of the things she said in the past".

"I'm not someone that likes to jump into controversial things or this political stuff. But I mean, you know, you never know," Irankunda said.

"One day I could be on the phone with her or sitting in an office chatting to her. So I mean … we'll see what happens."

Pauline Hanson's speech at the National Press Club included a call to end Australia's decades-old policy of multiculturalism. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

After her press club speech, Hanson said the Socceroos represented her vision of a monocultural Australia.

"People from different background and cultures and nations all wearing the green and gold and representing one nation under one flag and succeeding under the same set of rules," Hanson said in the Senate in June.

Socceroo Awer Mabil addressed the monoculture debate when he returned in July from the tournament, declaring his team was not distracted and that it was "all bullshit" to suggest Australia was not a multicultural society.

Australian team destined to 'go far'

Irankunda said despite the Round of 32 loss to Egypt, the Socceroos had youth on their side and could go further into the tournament.

"You can see now with the likes of Lucas Herrington, Ali [Alessandro] Circati, Jordy Bos, you know, Mohamed Touré, all these names, all these young boys coming through, including myself," Irankunda said.

"There's still a lot of talent coming through in Australia right now.

"Only time will tell how far we can go. But I feel like in my heart that we can go pretty far."

World.title: 'Embarassed and ashamed': Swans CEO explains decision to ban players
World.content:
The Sydney Swans say their willingness to "torpedo" their AFL season by suspending five star players proves how committed they are to upholding standards at the club.

The Swans suspended Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner for the remainder of the 2026 AFL season over an alleged incident at a Melbourne hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

At least five players were linked to an ongoing Victoria Police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, where the Swans were staying after their win over Essendon on Sunday night.

It is not suggested that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault and none of the banned players have been formally interviewed by police, according to the club, or charged.

In addition to the club sanction, the five Swans players will not be considered for All Australian selection, according to the AFL.

"Following the decision and appropriate club sanction imposed by the Sydney Swans today in relation to the conduct of five of their players, the AFL has determined those players will not be considered for selection in the 2026 All Australian squad," the league said in a statement.

"This decision is independent of the ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The AFL said the 2026 All Australian squad would be finalised on Monday next week, with the team announced at the AFL Awards the next day in Melbourne.

Telstra has spoken out, saying it was "deeply concerned by what's been reported" and respected that the matter was being investigated by police.

"Players assisting police with their investigation who are also Telstra ambassadors are not participating in any ambassador activity while the investigation is ongoing," a Telstra spokesperson said.

"We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time."

It is understood that Heeney and Warner have both been Telstra ambassadors.

Swans sponsors QBE came out in support of the club's actions.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson said today.

"We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club's position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women.

"Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further."

Another club sponsor, realestate.com.au, also responded, saying they were "deeply concerned about the serious allegations involving several Sydney Swans players".

"We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations," a company spokesperson said.

Swans sanctions solely for breaches of club standards

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney have been stood down. (ABC News/Getty Images)

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich have stressed the decision to ban the players is solely related to breaches of the club's standards and expected behaviour.

"Hopefully people can see how seriously we've taken this matter," Pridham said.

"We're very proud of our culture we've built over many years at the club. We get more right than we get wrong. Clearly this is a very sad day for us and for everybody involved.

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich (left) and chairman Andrew Pridham. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"I know the five players involved, they're extremely remorseful for their actions in breaching the club's standards, and I think the sanction we've imposed and the impact that will have on our football season is clear for all to see.

"It's very important to note the football outcome was not a consideration of the board."

Sydney's sanctions came after the club conducted interviews with the players linked to the Melbourne incident off-site with their lawyers present. Sydney's board met on Tuesday night to discuss club-imposed sanctions.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

The bans handed to the players, according to the club bosses, relate to their decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women back to the hotel.

Pavlich said it fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players", and Pridham added that their actions left the club with no choice but to impose a heavy sanction.

"They shouldn't have been in that situation," Pridham said.

"The only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we've done. To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this tells you how seriously we're taking this."

The AFL has backed the team's sanctions and the Swans say their decision is independent of an ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The rest of the Swans will prepare for North Melbourne on Sunday and then a finals campaign. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The players' ban includes this Sunday's home-and-away finale against North Melbourne and any finals matches the Swans will play afterwards.

Pavlich said the club was "deeply embarrassed and ashamed", stressing they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare and wellbeing of the women involved.

"They're the ones who are impacted severely at the moment," he said, adding that the Swans did not want to interfere with the police investigation by reaching out to the women directly.

While the five suspended players will not be allowed to play for the rest of the year, Pavlich said "they will be allowed back at the football club" this season.

"We're not abandoning our players," he said.

"We are supporting our players through this really challenging time for them."

Pridham pointed out the sanctions should not tarnish the entire team's reputation.

"There are many players this doesn't apply to, and I believe our male team has, by and large, displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something of concern," he said.

"However, clearly when situations such as this emerge, and clearly there has been a breakdown in standards, we will, in time, as a board and as an executive team, review how we deal with these things going forward and we'll look to see if changes need to be made.

"We're very, very proud of our culture. We don't get everything perfectly right over time, and things happen from time to time, and it's how we fix it going forward."

West Coast AFLW head coach Daisy Pearce has called on men to "be a good human" not just for themselves but for the effect they have on others. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

AFLW pioneer Daisy Pearce says it is "disappointing" allegations of violence against women have arisen again in the AFL.

Speaking at a press conference, West Coast Eagles AFLW coach Pearce urged young men to consider how their behaviour impacted others.

"Be a good human. Be a good human and for those that are in high-profile positions understand that you being a good human matters but it also has a massive impact on what other people think is acceptable as well," she said.

Swans team has always shown respect for women, Pridham says On a question about whether any changes are going to be made at the club going forward, Pridham says the male team has "by and large, always displayed complete respect for women". "I'd just highlight that this breach of our standards relates to five players. So, there are many players who this doesn't apply to," he said. "However, clearly, when situations such as this emerge – and clearly, there has been a breakdown in standards – we will, in time – as a board, and as an executive team – we will review how we deal with these things going forward." Club to be in a 'better position going forward', Pridham says Pridham has taken a question about whether he believes the Swans' season is now "torpedoed". "I think you've always got to enter the field of play with the expectation of performing well," he said. He says the fact that the club is willing to ban "five of our absolute best players" from the rest of the season shows it's "not trying to brush anything under the carpet". "I'm confident that, having taken this action, we'll be in a better place going forward as a result of it," he said. Show more

World.title: FIFA accused of 'management by fear' after key executive's sudden exit
World.content:
The head of Norwegian football has accused FIFA of fear tactics for the removal of a senior official who publicly opposed FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-withdrawn World Cup sell-off plan.

Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian Football Federation since 2022, told the Associated Press that the firing of FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour was "unacceptable" and urged other senior leaders to resist potentially damaging orders.

Mr Lamour's exit on Tuesday (AEST) came 17 days after his statement to AP criticising Mr Infantino's $US20 billion ($28.1 billion) private equity project, which was withdrawn hours later.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"Now he is thrown out and we are supposed to move on. It's unacceptable, it's management by fear," Ms Klaveness told the AP in a telephone interview, describing Mr Lamour as "the best football administrator I have ever met".

"Now we also have to call upon FIFA leadership and the administration to not submit to orders you know are not in the interests of football," Ms Klaveness added, especially targeting FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafström.

Ms Klaveness represented Norway 73 times as a player, is a judge in Oslo and an elected executive committee member at European football body UEFA.

She has built on her country's long-held reputation as a champion of good governance in soccer.

Last week the Norwegian federation's board called on Mr Infantino to resign and has backed a London-based NGO's formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators about his political ties to US President Donald Trump.

Mr Lamour was a long-time colleague of Mr Infantino, first when they were senior officials at UEFA from 2007-15. He was involved in Mr Infantino's campaign to be elected FIFA president in 2016 and moved two years ago from UEFA to oversee much of FIFA's operations in Zurich.

Infantino in crisis

Kevin Lamour (centre) said FIFA staff were "deceived" by the World Cup sell-off plan. (Getty Images: Richard Sellers)

With a reputation among the most trusted executives in the often murky world of global football politics, Mr Lamour's pointed criticisms of Mr Infantino's leadership intensified a crisis for the FIFA president.

A backlash from UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and north American soccer body CONCACAF was provoked by a secretive plan to sell future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

A $4.2 billion investment to take a 20 per cent stake in a FIFA commercial spin-off was to fund offers of $20 million to each of its 211 national member federations.

They already effectively own the non-profit soccer body, which has multi-billion dollar reserves, and would have had a mid-September deadline to accept.

Mr Lamour's statement on July 31 spoke of FIFA staff being "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness over the now-failed sale and how they "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

The French executive called on soccer leaders worldwide "to make the right decisions".

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he said at the conclusion of the statement.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

'A firing situation'

Lise Klaveness with Gianni Infantino at last month's FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

Ms Klaveness said Mr Lamour's exit was "a firing situation, it's not a resignation", and suggested it was done as a result of Mr Grafström "obviously being pressured by the president".

FIFA didn't respond to a request for comment on Ms Klaveness's remarks.

In a statement, FIFA said it "thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter".

Mr Lamour did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on Wednesday (AEST).

"His statement was necessary to kill the project," Ms Klaveness said of Mr Lamour's intervention.

" He said something that was obvious, that was very important that someone within the staff told us the story so that we knew it was not FIFA, as such, but one person. "

Mr Infantino held a meeting with senior management — minus Mr Lamour — in Rabat, Morocco on August 5.

Following that, FIFA issued a statement apologising for errors and said those managers who attended "reaffirmed their full support" for Mr Infantino's presidency.

"We all got reports in Morocco, we know it's a management of fear," Ms Klaveness said.

"It's not in football's best interests."

Until the uproar over Mr Infantino's "FIFA Forward Enterprise" proposal, he seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next year in Morocco for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

Challengers have until November 18 to enter the contest.

Norway not discussing other candidates

Though UEFA and other critics of Mr Infantino want him ousted from the $6 million-per-year FIFA job, Ms Klaveness said any search for an opponent was not a talking point in Norway.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We are not there at all and that is 100 per cent the truth," she said, adding that any candidate would have to be "very accountable to a governance structure that will not in four or five years just deteriorate".

Mr Infantino was appointed by UEFA in 2015 to a panel advising FIFA on reforms, in fallout from corruption scandals provoked by US federal investigations.

That group's recommendations limiting FIFA presidents to 12 years in office, plus limiting their executive powers and patronage all have retreated under Mr Infantino.

Ms Klaveness acknowledged FIFA members had been less "passionate about the details of governance" than Norway.

Mr Lamour also won praise and support from UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister, also a former player and now a university professor of governance in Wales, who lamented the "shabby events of the past weeks".

"Kevin's sacking seriously weakens FIFA's administration whilst undermining this unique opportunity to shift the culture at FIFA and to reset the organisation on sporting values, not simply commercial and financial ones," Ms McAllister said.

World.title: Dees star's ban upheld as AFL tribunal rejects biomechanist evidence bid
World.content:
Melbourne has suffered a major pre-finals blow, potentially losing key forward Jacob van Rooyen for the rest of the AFL season through suspension.

The Demons failed in their bid to have van Rooyen's three-game ban for striking overturned or reduced.

It means he will miss the fifth-placed Demons' final home-and-away game on Saturday against the Western Bulldogs, and that Melbourne will need to win two finals for him to play again this season.

Van Rooyen is having a career-best season, kicking 42 goals in 22 games.

The Demons forward was charged with striking after he concussed Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir in a marking contest on Saturday night at the Adelaide Oval. It was graded as severe impact, careless conduct and high impact.

After the 90-minute hearing, where van Rooyen testified that he was trying to mark the ball when he collected Aliir, the tribunal jury deliberated for nearly an hour before upholding the charge.

Melbourne had argued van Rooyen's attempt to mark the ball was not careless, but the tribunal rejected their case.

Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC also turned down a bid from the Demons to have a biomechanist give evidence for van Rooyen.

Aliir Aliir was left concussed after being struck in the head by van Rooyen's swinging arm. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

"The swing of van Rooyen's left arm constituted the act of a strike. It was a forceful blow. It was not simply a trailing or leading arm that Aliir collided with," Gleeson said in the verdict, adding the panel found it was careless.

"Van Rooyen was initially intending to mark the ball, but we find that shortly before impact, he ceased to intend to mark the ball. We say this despite van Rooyen's evidence to the contrary.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Even if it was van Rooyen's sole objective at all times to contest the mark, we find that he did so in a way that failed to take reasonable care to avoid acts which could be reasonably foreseen to result in a reportable offence.

"Van Rooyen had time to move his right arm in response to seeing Aliir and he could have done so to some extent or sufficient extent with his left arm."

The tribunal also found the impact was severe and said there was potential for further injury, such as a facial fracture.

Also on Tuesday night, Brisbane AFLW key forward Dakota Davidson failed to have her one-game striking ban downgraded.

The Lions pleaded guilty and tried to argue the clash with Essendon's Maddi Gay was low rather than medium impact, but the AFLW tribunal upheld the grading.

It means one of the league's top forwards will miss the grand final rematch against two-time defending premiers North Melbourne.

World.title: Venus Williams receives US Open wildcard at 46, Serena may follow
World.content:
Venus Williams has received a US Open singles wild card and the tournament is keeping one on hold, perhaps in case her sister Serena wants to join her.

Sloane Stephens, the 2017 US Open champion, was one of six other women to receive a wild card, and the US Tennis Association said the final one was still to be announced.

That will almost certainly go to Serena Williams if she decides she wants to return to the tournament at 44.

Venus Williams received a wild card last year, returning to the grand slam event she won twice for the first time since 2023. The 46-year-old has become the oldest entrant in singles at the tournament since Renee Richards played at 47 in 1981, according to the International Tennis Federation.

Serena Williams could make her return to Flushing Meadows via the final wildcard spot. (Getty Images: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport)

She has continued to play some singles matches, and this week joined Serena for their first doubles tournament together since the 2022 US Open. They lost at the Cincinnati Open in a match tiebreaker against Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns.

The sisters planned to play at Wimbledon but had to withdraw after Serena injured her knee in her singles match. That marked her first time playing singles since the 2022 US Open, and she indicated afterwards that she hoped to keep competing if she was healthy.

Headlining the wild-card recipients on the men's side are 39-year-old Gael Monfils, a past US Open semifinalist who is set to play his final grand slam tournament before retiring, and Australian Alexei Popyrin, who upset Novak Djokovic in 2024 on the way to the fourth round.

One spot is also being held among the eight men's wild cards. Stan Wawrinka, the 2016 champion at Flushing Meadows, who at 41 is playing his final season, could be a candidate for that.

Australia's Alexei Popyrin has received one of the wildcards in the men's draw. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/David Kirouac)

Also receiving women's wild cards were Carol Young Suh Lee, Reese Brantmeier, Thea Frodin, Leolia Jeanjean and Taylah Preston.

The other men receiving wild cards were two-time reigning NCAA singles champion Michael Zheng, Martin Damm, JJ Wolf, Sebastian Gorzny and Jack Kennedy.

Kei Nishikori, the 2014 US Open runner-up who also is retiring, was given a wild card into the men's qualifying tournament, along with Jordan Lee, Trevor Svajda, Andre Ilagan, Spencer Johnson, Michael Antonius, Andrew Johnson and Daniel Milavsky.

Women given spots in the qualifying tournament were Caroline Dolehide, Janae Preston, Katrina Scott, Ayana Akli, Annika Penickova, Julieta Pareja, Kristina Penickova and Savannah Broadus.

The main draw begins on August 30, with the qualifying tournaments being played earlier that week.

World.title: Darts club membership booms as miners create 'great little community'
World.content:
While darts is typically known as a pub game to some, it is so much more.

"You don't have to be the best; you just come in, have a beer, listen to music, throw some darts."

Owen Thompson is the Moranbah Darts Club secretary.

The club gets together during the week for a social throw and also host regular competitions and events to raise money for local charities. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

On a wintry Tuesday night, the darts hall in the regional mining town in central Queensland is filling up.

Mates greet each other with a handshake and a slap on the back as the sound of beer cans opening rings through the air.

"I'm no good at it. I just come here every Tuesday to throw stuff at the board and have a few beers," Mr Thompson said.

Loading...

In the town, about 200 kilometres south-west of Mackay, the previous club closed down a few years ago, but the dedication and perseverance of a few members has brought it back to life.

The club now hosts weekly social nights, regular tournaments and charity fundraising events.

"We gradually grew from no-one … to 60 members last season," Mr Thompson said.

Mining country

Moranbah is the largest town in the Isaac region, surrounded by dozens of coal mines. (ABC News: Peter Mullins)

Moranbah is the heartland of coal country in the Bowen Basin.

While the town's official population is 9,425 people (2021 Census), it has a transient workforce that flies, drives or buses in and out of the 47 mines across the Bowen Basin, 30 of which are in the Isaac region.

With long shift-work hours, playing darts has become a source of solace.

"For me personally, I was not doing real well mentally. I found the boys. We come together, clear your head, gives you something to do, gives you a bit of worth," Mr Thompson said.

Fellow club member and vice-president Quinton "Quinno" McCormick constantly tries to recruit his mining mates to have a throw and get out of the mine "camp life".

"We really push the mental health side of things for the people who are away [from] their families … it's just a little somewhere they can escape and live a normal life for a little bit," he said.

It is for anyone who wants to have a go.

Taz and Cassandra Whiteley at the Moranbah darts hall. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Moranbah newcomer Cassandra Whiteley says it is "something different", and its appeal to various fitness levels is a bonus.

"It doesn't have to be high intensity," she said.

"Something different … I enjoy it; it can be as competitive or as fun as you want it to be."

Ms Whiteley, who moved to the town in early 2025, is one of the few female players at the club.

"When we first moved over here, we didn't know a lot of people. I was away at work on training, and my husband actually found the darts place and came down here," she said.

It took three months before she picked up a dart.

"They're a really great group of guys and everyone's lovely, and it's good to get out of the house and have people to talk to and people that genuinely care.

"They're a really great little community here."

Taz Whiteley has competed in darts competitions across Queensland. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Husband Wade Whiteley, known locally as "Taz", a nod to his Tasmanian roots, played competitively in his younger years.

He passes on his tips and tricks to the newcomers.

"Keep your body still, throw with your arm, not your whole body," he said.

"Teaching them rhythm, how to count, a lot of it's counting. Ninety per cent of the game is math, knowing where to go next and not having to stop."

For those keen to take it a bit further than the pub, the World Darts Federation hold its international championship annually.

While darts is not currently featured in the Olympic or Commonwealth Games, Darts Australia has been lobbying to have it included in the latter.

The club uses electronic technology that automatically sends scores to a tablet on the wall. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Back in Moranbah, it is just about bullseyes and banter.

"I don't think I will be, no, [entering the Commonwealth Games]," Mr Thompson said.

"There's a couple that probably think they can; we'll see if they can prove it."

Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Robin Williams’ children are taking over their father’s Instagram account after his daughter spoke out against the use of his AI likeness, as reported earlier by The Wrap. In a post on Tuesday, Zak, Zelda, and Cody Williams write that they want the late actor’s Instagram profile to be a “safe, trusted place where the stories, photos, videos, and memories shared reflect his legacy with authenticity, warmth, and care.”

A story posted to Zelda Williams’ own Instagram account expands on the decision to bring back her father’s profile, saying that it’s meant to help combat “rampant AI abuse,” according to The Wrap:

I’m sorry if anyone found Dad’s old page posting again to be triggering. Believe me, I know it’s a little strange. Making that space into one where people can find authentic clips and photos of him is one of the best ways we’ve now found to fight back against rampant AI abuse of his voice and likeness on here.

Robin Williams’ Instagram account remained inactive following his death in 2014. Last year, Zelda Williams asked fans to stop sending her AI-generated videos of her father. “To watch the legacies of real people be condensed down to ‘this vaguely looks and sounds like them so that’s enough’, just so other people can churn out horrible TikTok slop puppeteering them is maddening,” she wrote at the time.

Though some AI chatbots have restrictions in place to prevent users from generating images or videos with the AI likeness of a public figure or celebrity, these guardrails can still be bypassed. OpenAI’s now-shuttered Sora app became a hotbed for generating videos of copyrighted characters and celebrities, while Grok is still generating sexualized AI deepfakes of famous women, according to Wired.

Zelda, Zak, and Cody Williams add that they’re going to use their father’s Instagram account to share his “unique talent and humor with the world.”

Tech.title: OpenAI lays out new security changes after its AI hacked Hugging Face
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is announcing security updates following the July news that its AI broke out of a sandboxed environment and accidentally hacked Hugging Face, including improvements to its research environments, monitoring, and alignment techniques. The company had already put the brakes on a new model, Astra, that it thinks could have “critical” cybersecurity capabilities, and the company says it instituted a two-week pause in reinforcement learning (RL) training on its “latest models intended for deployment” while it tightened up security. The company’s “largest planned frontier RL run remains on hold.”

For its frontier model research, OpenAI now requires stronger sandboxes for workloads that “execute model-generated or otherwise untrusted code,” and has more controls to “isolate higher-risk and untrusted workloads from the internet.” It has also updated its research environment to “remove potentially vulnerable shared services, reduce standing privileges, and improve security and trust boundaries.”

As part of the company’s expanded monitoring setup, OpenAI now aims to issue an alert “within 30 minutes after concerning activity is surfaced,” OpenAI says. If the people paged after an alert can’t “conclusively” determine whether an alert is a false positive within 30 minutes, “those teams are expected to pause the activity.”

OpenAI also says that it’s applying “our core alignment techniques across more stages of the training process,” including reward models that “better detect and discourage unsafe behavior” and training models “to be more honest about their actions, capabilities, and limitations.”

Since the discovery of the Hugging Face breach, Anthropic and Meta have also found that their AI models had hacked other organizations.
